options.C: It evaluates the structural integrity of the patient's skin barriers
options.D: It identifies gaps in acquired adaptive immunity against preventable diseases

explanation: Vaccination history reveals whether a host has developed specific protective antibodies against targeted pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T4#GNS313_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is the main community benefit of achieving high immunization coverage in a population?

options.A: Eradicating bacterial agents from municipal water supplies
options.B: Establishing herd immunity to protect vulnerable non-vaccinated individuals
options.C: Curing chronic nutritional deficiencies in school-age children
options.D: Eliminating all environmental vectors of disease transmission permanently

explanation: High vaccination rates reduce the spread of pathogens through a population, indirectly protecting those who cannot receive vaccines. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T4#GNS313_U1_T4_h7)

question: Which public health intervention directly targets a major nutritional vulnerability in young children?

options.A: Routine screening of blood pressure in adult populations
options.B: Vitamin A supplementation and therapeutic food distribution
options.C: Distribution of insecticide-treated mosquito nets
options.D: Construction of modern drainage channels in urban markets

explanation: Targeted nutritional programs supply essential micronutrients and macronutrients needed to maintain mucosal immunity and tissue integrity. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T4#GNS313_U1_T4_h7)

question: What term describes the natural habitat where a pathogen lives and multiplies?

options.A: Portal of exit
options.B: Susceptible host
options.C: Reservoir
options.D: Infectious agent

explanation: A reservoir serves as the primary home and source where pathogens survive and reproduce before moving to a new host. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why must nurses understand all links in the chain of infection?

options.A: To effectively break the cycle and prevent disease spread
options.B: To determine the financial cost of hospital admissions
options.C: To accurately diagnose the specific strain of bacteria
options.D: To calculate the exact incubation period for every patient

explanation: Interrupting any single link in the chain stops the transmission of infectious agents to vulnerable patients. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h1)

question: A non-living surrounding that supports the survival of a pathogen is called what?

options.A: An infectious agent
options.B: An environmental reservoir
options.C: A susceptible host
options.D: A human carrier

explanation: Soil, water, and food act as non-living environmental reservoirs where certain pathogens thrive. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h2)

question: Why is identifying the reservoir critical for disease control?

options.A: It targets the primary source where pathogens live and multiply
options.B: It guarantees immediate immunity for all exposed hospital staff
options.C: It shortens the standard antibiotic treatment duration for patients
options.D: It eliminates the need for standard hand hygiene practices

explanation: Directing control measures at the source of the pathogen prevents further spread into the community or ward. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is an individual called who harbors a pathogen without ever showing symptoms?

options.A: An asymptomatic carrier
options.B: A convalescent case
options.C: An active patient
options.D: A susceptible host

explanation: Asymptomatic carriers spread infections unknowingly because they appear completely healthy while shedding the pathogen. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h3)

question: A patient recovering from typhoid fever continues to shed bacteria in stool samples. What type of human reservoir is this?

options.A: Environmental source
options.B: Active clinical case
options.C: Convalescent carrier
options.D: Zoonotic host

explanation: Convalescent carriers shed infectious agents during the recovery phase after their acute symptoms have disappeared. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is an infectious disease that is transmissible from animals to humans called?

options.A: A genetic disorder
options.B: An endogenous illness
options.C: A zoonotic disease
options.D: A nosocomial infection

explanation: Zoonotic diseases naturally pass between vertebrate animals and human populations. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why do animal reservoirs pose a unique challenge for public health eradication efforts?

options.A: Wild animal populations are difficult to isolate, vaccinate, or monitor
options.B: Animals always show severe symptoms when they carry dangerous human pathogens
options.C: Zoonotic pathogens never survive outside an animal host for more than an hour
options.D: Livestock are immune to all forms of bacterial and viral infections

explanation: Controlling disease in wild animal reservoirs is practically impossible compared to treating infected human populations. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which bacterium found commonly in soil causes tetanus after entering a puncture wound?

options.A: Vibrio cholerae
options.B: Salmonella typhi
options.C: Clostridium tetani
options.D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

explanation: Clostridium tetani spores live in soil and dust, entering the body through broken skin barriers. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h5)

question: A patient steps on a rusty nail in a farm field. Which environmental reservoir is the primary source of the risk?

options.A: Food
options.B: Soil
options.C: Air
options.D: Water

explanation: Soil is the natural environmental reservoir for tetanus spores found frequently around farms and rusty metal outdoors. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h5)

question: What is an inanimate object like a contaminated thermometer or bed rail called?

options.A: A vector
options.B: A carrier
options.C: A zoonosis
options.D: A fomite

explanation: Fomites are non-living objects that transfer pathogens between patients if disinfection protocols are missed. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h6)

question: A mosquito transmits the malaria parasite from one person to another. What role does the mosquito play?

options.A: Portal of entry
options.B: Fomite
options.C: Reservoir
options.D: Vector

explanation: Arthropods like mosquitoes act as biological vectors carrying parasites between human hosts. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h6)

question: Why is proper disinfection of medical equipment crucial in ward management?

options.A: It eliminates the need for nurses to wear sterile gloves
options.B: It transforms airborne pathogens into harmless water droplets
options.C: It prevents inanimate objects from acting as fomite reservoirs
options.D: It permanently cures chronic infections in human carriers

explanation: Cleaning and disinfecting equipment removes pathogens that otherwise colonize surfaces and spread to patients. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h7)

question: Which nursing action directly targets human reservoirs to prevent hospital outbreaks?

options.A: Sprinkling chemical disinfectants across public walkways
options.B: Placing infected patients in appropriate isolation precautions
options.C: Leaving medical waste uncovered in patient hallways
options.D: Stopping all routine handwashing procedures on the ward

explanation: Isolation precautions contain infectious agents within known human cases to protect others on the ward. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T5#GNS313_U1_T5_h7)

question: What does the route of transmission describe in epidemiology?

options.A: The speed at which a disease kills human cells
options.B: The total number of immune people in a town
options.C: The pathway a pathogen takes to reach a host
options.D: The time a germ spends growing inside an animal

explanation: The route of transmission specifically tracks the path an infectious agent uses to travel from a source to a new host. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why must nurses understand how a specific pathogen travels?

options.A: To choose the correct barrier protection and isolation rules
options.B: To calculate the exact monetary cost of treating patients
options.C: To write medical discharge summaries for pharmacy staff
options.D: To decide which surgical instruments need immediate sharpening

explanation: Knowing the transmission path allows nurses to apply targeted precautions like masks or gloves to stop the spread. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h1)

question: Name the link in the chain of infection that involves respiratory secretions leaving the body.

options.A: Natural reservoir
options.B: Portal of exit
options.C: Susceptible host
options.D: Infectious agent

explanation: Secretions act as a portal of exit allowing the pathogen to leave the infected reservoir. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h2)

question: An unvaccinated patient who easily catches measles represents which part of the chain?

options.A: Mode of transmission
options.B: Portal of entry
options.C: Infectious agent
options.D: Susceptible host

explanation: A person who lacks immunity and can easily contract the disease fills the susceptible host link. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which infection is typically spread through direct physical contact?

options.A: Cholera
options.B: Malaria
options.C: Scabies
options.D: Tuberculosis

explanation: Scabies is caused by mites that pass directly from skin to skin during close contact. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h3)

question: A nurse cares for a patient with open skin lesions without wearing gloves. What transmission risk is highest?

options.A: Airborne droplet nuclei spread
options.B: Common vehicle waterborne spread
options.C: Direct contact transmission
options.D: Vector-borne mosquito transmission

explanation: Touching open skin lesions without gloves exposes the nurse to direct contact transmission of pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is an inanimate object that transfers infectious agents called?

options.A: Carrier
options.B: Fomite
options.C: Vector
options.D: Reservoir

explanation: Inanimate objects like equipment or furniture that carry germs are known as fomites. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why are shared stethoscopes a major concern for indirect contact transmission?

options.A: They attract insects that carry bloodborne parasites into wards
options.B: They release toxic chemicals that weaken the patient immune system
options.C: They generate airborne droplets during routine blood pressure checks
options.D: They touch multiple patients without being cleaned between uses

explanation: Using the same stethoscope on different patients without disinfection transfers pathogens from one person to another indirectly. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h4)

question: Which disease is primarily spread through airborne droplet nuclei?

options.A: Tuberculosis
options.B: Gonorrhea
options.C: Malaria
options.D: Cholera

explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis travels on tiny airborne nuclei that remain suspended in the air for hours. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h5)

question: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is admitted. Which protective measure should the nurse prioritize?

options.A: Provide disposable utensils and ensure food is served on paper plates
options.B: Wipe down all metal bed rails with a chlorine solution every two hours
options.C: Give the patient a surgical mask and restrict visitors to immediate family members
options.D: Place the patient in a room with special air ventilation and wear an N95 mask

explanation: Airborne pathogens require specialized ventilation and respiratory protection like N95 masks to prevent inhalation. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h5)

question: Which living organism acts as the biological vector for malaria?

options.A: Mosquito
options.B: Tick
options.C: Housefly
options.D: Rat

explanation: Female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit the malaria parasite through their bites. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h6)

question: What distinguishes a biological vector from a mechanical vector?

options.A: Mechanical vectors bite humans while biological vectors only walk on food
options.B: The pathogen undergoes development or multiplication inside the biological vector
options.C: The biological vector is always an insect while mechanical vectors are animals
options.D: Pathogens cannot survive on mechanical vectors for more than a few minutes

explanation: Biological vectors actively support the life cycle of the pathogen, whereas mechanical vectors merely transport it on their exterior. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which disease is typically acquired through common vehicle waterborne transmission?

options.A: Tuberculosis
options.B: Cholera
options.C: Scabies
options.D: Measles

explanation: Cholera outbreaks usually occur when drinking water sources become contaminated with sewage containing Vibrio cholerae. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h7)

question: A community experiences a sudden outbreak of watery diarrhea after drinking from a shared river source. What type of transmission is most likely occurring?

options.A: Direct contact transmission
options.B: Vector-borne transmission
options.C: Airborne droplet transmission
options.D: Common vehicle transmission

explanation: When many people fall ill from a single contaminated source like a shared water supply, it represents common vehicle transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of contact tracing during a disease outbreak?

options.A: To identify and monitor individuals exposed to an infected person
options.B: To test the municipal water supply for bacterial contamination
options.C: To vaccinate the entire population against every known virus
options.D: To clean and disinfect all medical equipment in the hospital ward

explanation: Contact tracing finds people who had contact with an index case to monitor them and prevent further spread. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h8)

question: Which nursing intervention directly protects a susceptible host from vector-borne disease?

options.A: Checking blood pressure twice daily
options.B: Isolating patients in negative pressure rooms
options.C: Distributing insecticide-treated bed nets
options.D: Performing surgical hand scrubs

explanation: Bed nets shield people from mosquito bites, protecting susceptible hosts from vector-borne malaria. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T6#GNS313_U1_T6_h8)

question: What represents the starting point in the chain of infection?

options.A: Source of infection
options.B: Portal of entry
options.C: Susceptible host
options.D: Mode of transmission

explanation: The source of infection acts as the origin where the infectious agent lives and multiplies before moving to a new host. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why must every link in the chain of infection remain intact?

options.A: To allow the disease to transmit successfully
options.B: To prevent the immune system from responding
options.C: To speed up the incubation period of bacteria
options.D: To guarantee complete recovery of the patient

explanation: If any single link in the chain is broken, the infectious agent cannot reach or infect a new host. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h1)

question: What is the natural home where a germ normally lives and multiplies called?

options.A: Fomite
options.B: Reservoir
options.C: Vector
options.D: Carrier

explanation: A reservoir is the natural habitat where an organism survives and multiplies over time. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h2)

question: How does a source of infection differ from a reservoir?

options.A: The reservoir is always an inanimate object while the source is living
options.B: The source is the immediate point from which the germ transfers to a host
options.C: The reservoir is the final destination of the infectious agent
options.D: The source only harbors viruses while the reservoir harbors bacteria

explanation: The source is where the infection is directly caught, whereas the reservoir is the broader, long-term home for the germ. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h2)

question: Which human source harbors a pathogen without ever showing signs of illness?

options.A: Clinical case
options.B: Index patient
options.C: Healthy carrier
options.D: Convalescent case

explanation: Healthy carriers shed infectious agents into the environment without experiencing any clinical symptoms themselves. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h3)

question: What makes convalescent carriers a major challenge in infection control?

options.A: They refuse to isolate because they feel physically strong
options.B: They display more severe symptoms than primary clinical cases
options.C: They are completely immune to standard antibiotic treatments
options.D: They continue shedding germs even after recovering from symptoms

explanation: Convalescent carriers look and feel healthy, leading others to let down their guard while they still spread microbes. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h3)

question: What term describes infections that spread naturally from animals to humans?

options.A: Iatrogenic illnesses
options.B: Zoonotic diseases
options.C: Nosocomial infections
options.D: Opportunistic infections

explanation: Zoonoses are infections shared between animals and human populations under natural conditions. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h4)

question: A cholera outbreak linked to a flooded community stream demonstrates which type of source?

options.A: Iatrogenic source
options.B: Healthy human carrier
options.C: Zoonotic vector
options.D: Environmental source

explanation: Contaminated water supplies and soil represent environmental reservoirs and sources of waterborne germs. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h4)

question: What is the first case identified in a disease outbreak called?

options.A: Secondary source
options.B: Terminal host
options.C: Primary carrier
options.D: Index case

explanation: The index case is the first patient brought to the attention of epidemiologists during an investigation. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why is tracing the source of an infection critical during a hospital ward outbreak?

options.A: To assign legal blame to specific staff members
options.B: To determine the financial cost of patient care
options.C: To eliminate the need for routine hand hygiene
options.D: To stop further transmission by isolating the origin

explanation: Finding the source allows nurses and infection control teams to implement targeted barriers and stop the spread. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h5)

question: Which nursing action directly neutralizes a human source of bacterial infection?

options.A: Applying hand sanitizer after meals
options.B: Educating patients on balanced diets
options.C: Placing surgical masks on visitors
options.D: Administering prescribed antibiotics

explanation: Effective antimicrobial therapy kills the pathogen within the human source, stopping active shedding. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h6)

question: Why is isolating an infectious patient considered a primary source-control measure?

options.A: It boosts the immune system of healthcare workers
options.B: It disinfects the air inside the hospital room
options.C: It cures the patient of the underlying disease faster
options.D: It physically separates the source from susceptible hosts

explanation: Isolation stops the pathogen from bridging the gap between the infected source and uninfected individuals. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T7#GNS313_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary function of primary lymphoid organs like the thymus?

options.A: Production and maturation of lymphocytes
options.B: Filtering bacteria directly from the bloodstream
options.C: Storing excess platelets for clotting events
options.D: Producing red blood cells for oxygen transport

explanation: Primary lymphoid organs are specifically responsible for creating and maturing immune cells like T and B lymphocytes before they encounter antigens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why is the ability to distinguish between self and non-self molecules essential?

options.A: It allows the body to absorb nutrients efficiently from food
options.B: It stops foreign pathogens from entering the lymphatic vessels
options.C: It accelerates the production of red blood cells in bone marrow
options.D: It prevents the immune system from attacking healthy body tissue

explanation: Recognizing self from non-self ensures that immune responses target actual invaders rather than causing autoimmune damage to the body. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h1)

question: How does innate immunity differ from adaptive immunity regarding response time?

options.A: Both systems respond at the exact same speed during an active infection
options.B: Innate immunity takes weeks to develop, while adaptive immunity works instantly
options.C: Innate immunity responds immediately, whereas adaptive immunity has a delayed response
options.D: Innate immunity only activates after adaptive memory cells have been depleted

explanation: Innate mechanisms are pre-existing and react instantly to injury, while adaptive immunity requires time to identify and multiply against specific antigens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h2)

question: A key characteristic that distinguishes adaptive immunity from innate immunity is...

options.A: The presence of long-term immunological memory
options.B: Dependence on physical barriers like the skin
options.C: Being completely absent at the time of birth
options.D: Using non-specific phagocytes to clear debris

explanation: Adaptive immunity records previous encounters with pathogens to provide faster and stronger protection upon subsequent exposures, which innate immunity lacks. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h2)

question: Natural active immunity is typically acquired through which of the following ways?

options.A: Receiving an injection of pre-formed antibodies
options.B: Transplacental transfer of maternal antibodies
options.C: Recovering from a natural microbial infection
options.D: Getting a routine vaccination at the clinic

explanation: Natural active immunity develops when a person is infected naturally and their own immune system creates antibodies and memory cells. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the primary advantage of artificial active immunity over natural active immunity?

options.A: It never requires booster doses to maintain lifetime effectiveness
options.B: It provides instant protection within minutes of receiving the dose
options.C: It confers protection without exposing the person to severe disease symptoms
options.D: It relies entirely on maternal antibodies passed down during gestation

explanation: Vaccines stimulate the immune system safely using killed or weakened agents, sparing individuals from the dangerous complications of full-blown natural infections. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h3)

question: How long does protection typically last when a patient receives passive immunity?

options.A: Only a few weeks or months
options.B: For the entire lifespan of the individual
options.C: Only for the duration of a single day
options.D: Exactly five to ten years after exposure

explanation: Because passive immunity relies on borrowed antibodies without memory cell formation, the protection fades as those antibodies naturally break down. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h4)

question: An infant receiving protective antibodies through breast milk is an example of...

options.A: Natural passive immunity
options.B: Artificial passive immunity
options.C: Natural active immunity
options.D: Artificial active immunity

explanation: Colostrum and breast milk supply ready-made maternal antibodies naturally to the nursing infant without requiring the infant's immune system to generate them. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is the primary benefit of achieving high levels of herd immunity in a population?

options.A: It completely eradicates all environmental pathogens instantly
options.B: It replaces the need for personal hygiene and sanitation
options.C: It guarantees that mutation of viruses will never occur
options.D: It protects vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated

explanation: Herd immunity shields those who cannot receive vaccines by drastically reducing the circulation of the infectious agent in the community. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why does a highly contagious disease require more people to be immune to achieve herd immunity?

options.A: Vulnerable populations are more numerous in areas with high transmission rates
options.B: Contagious pathogens are larger and easily destroyed by white blood cells
options.C: Easily spread pathogens require fewer susceptible hosts to keep outbreaks going
options.D: Vaccines for high-transmission diseases wear off much faster

explanation: Pathogens that spread easily from person to person need a denser network of immune individuals to successfully block transmission chains. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h5)

question: The gradual deterioration of immune competence in older adults is known as what?

options.A: Active suppression
options.B: Immunosenescence
options.C: Autoimmune depletion
options.D: Immunization failure

explanation: Immunosenescence describes the natural age-related decline in immune system function that leaves elderly populations more susceptible to infections. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h6)

question: How does severe protein malnutrition negatively affect a child's immune system?

options.A: It impairs lymphocyte function and decreases antibody production
options.B: It prevents the spleen from filtering red blood cells
options.C: It directly converts active immunity into passive immunity
options.D: It accelerates the breakdown of beneficial maternal antibodies

explanation: Adequate protein and nutrients are necessary building blocks for immune cells; deficiency leads to weakened defense mechanisms. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h6)

question: What is the standard temperature range for storing most routine vaccines in the cold chain?

options.A: Between +2°C and +8°C
options.B: Between -20°C and -10°C
options.C: Between +15°C and +25°C
options.D: Between +35°C and +40°C

explanation: Maintaining storage temperatures between +2°C and +8°C is vital to prevent heat degradation and preserve the immunological potency of standard vaccines. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why is proper cold chain management challenging during rural immunization outreaches in Nigeria?

options.A: Vaccines manufactured for tropical regions do not require temperature regulation
options.B: Vaccine vial monitors change color to indicate expiration rather than heat damage
options.C: Rural health facilities usually refuse to stock any form of biological products
options.D: Erratic electricity and transport difficulties threaten temperature control

explanation: Power supply inconsistencies and difficult terrain make maintaining a continuous cold chain during outreach activities a constant operational challenge. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a core responsibility of a community health nurse in immunization programs?

options.A: Manufacturing new viral strains for regional vaccine development
options.B: Monitoring and reporting adverse events following immunization
options.C: Administering vaccines safely and managing cold chain inventory
options.D: Educating mothers during antenatal visits to reduce vaccine hesitancy

explanation: Vaccine manufacturing takes place in specialized pharmaceutical laboratories, whereas community health nurses focus on education, delivery, and safety surveillance in the field. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h8)

question: Why is monitoring for adverse events following immunization a vital nursing task?

options.A: It proves that cold chain temperatures never fluctuate during transport
options.B: It helps maintain public trust and ensures patient safety by managing reactions promptly
options.C: It eliminates the need for community mobilization and health education
options.D: It converts artificial passive immunity into long-term active immunity

explanation: Monitoring side effects reassures the community that safety is a priority, preventing rumors and fear from derailing vaccination campaigns. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T8#GNS313_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the incubation period of an infectious disease?

options.A: Period between symptom onset and full recovery
options.B: Time from pathogen entry to first symptom appearance
options.C: Duration of time a patient remains contagious
options.D: Total lifespan of the pathogen inside the host

explanation: The incubation period is the time between when a pathogen enters the body and when the first symptoms show up. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why do patients feel healthy during the incubation period?

options.A: The pathogen population is still too low to cause visible disruption
options.B: Antibodies completely neutralize the organism during this phase
options.C: The immune system temporarily ignores the foreign microbe
options.D: Pathogens only multiply after symptoms begin showing

explanation: Symptoms only appear after the pathogen has multiplied enough to cause noticeable damage or toxin buildup. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h1)

question: What main activity happens during the incubation phase?

options.A: Rapid replication of the pathogen inside tissues
options.B: Immediate destruction of all host immune cells
options.C: Complete elimination of toxins by the liver
options.D: Instantaneous production of chronic antibodies

explanation: During this phase, microbes multiply and establish themselves in the host's body. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h2)

question: What causes the incubation period to end and illness to start?

options.A: Activation of the patient's adaptive memory cells
options.B: Pathogen load crossing a critical damage threshold
options.C: Spontaneous mutation of the microbe into a harmless form
options.D: The complete exhaustion of the host nutrient supply

explanation: Symptoms start when cellular injury and pathogen numbers reach a high enough level to trigger a bodily reaction. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h2)

question: A larger initial infectious dose typically causes the incubation period to be...

options.A: longer
options.B: unpredictable
options.C: unchanged
options.D: shorter

explanation: Starting with more organisms means less time is needed to reach the critical threshold for symptoms. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h3)

question: How does the route of entry affect how quickly a disease develops?

options.A: Direct blood access bypasses initial local multiplication delays
options.B: Oral ingestion guarantees a zero-day incubation timeframe
options.C: Inhalational entry stops all systemic immune reactions
options.D: Skin contact always prevents pathogens from entering the system

explanation: Pathogens that enter the bloodstream directly reach target organs faster than those that have to cross mucosal surfaces first. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h3)

question: What does the latent period measure in an infection?

options.A: Period between first symptom and full recovery
options.B: Total time the pathogen survives on environmental surfaces
options.C: Duration of time a patient stays in hospital isolation
options.D: Time from infection until the host becomes contagious

explanation: The latent period tracks the time it takes for an infected person to gain the ability to pass the infection to others. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h4)

question: Why is knowing the difference between incubation and latent periods important?

options.A: It explains why asymptomatic individuals can spread diseases
options.B: It dictates the required dosage for oral antibiotics
options.C: It proves that all pathogens share identical growth rates
options.D: It indicates the exact chemical composition of vaccines

explanation: When the latent period is shorter than the incubation period, people can spread the disease before they even realize they are sick. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h4)

question: What is a main public health use for calculating an incubation period?

options.A: Calculating the total number of immune people in a city
options.B: Predicting daily weather patterns that favor bacterial growth
options.C: Determining the exact financial cost of patient hospital care
options.D: Estimating the date of exposure during an outbreak investigation

explanation: Knowing the typical incubation time lets investigators work backward from when symptoms started to find out when exposure happened. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h5)

question: Several patients develop food poisoning at a wedding reception. Which metric helps investigators find the contaminated meal?

options.A: Incubation period
options.B: Convalescent window
options.C: Latent period
options.D: Seroconversion rate

explanation: Working backward using the known incubation window of the suspected pathogen points directly to the meal eaten at the event. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h5)

question: Quarantine duration for an exposed contact is determined by which disease characteristic?

options.A: Total recovery duration
options.B: Maximum incubation period
options.C: Pathogen physical size
options.D: Minimum latent window

explanation: Quarantine must last as long as the longest known incubation window to catch delayed-onset cases. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h6)

question: What happens if a contact leaves quarantine before the incubation period ends?

options.A: They will develop immunity without experiencing any illness
options.B: The pathogen instantly becomes non-infectious in their body
options.C: Their immune system automatically clears all remaining pathogens
options.D: They might develop symptoms and spread the disease in the community

explanation: Releasing someone too early risks missing individuals who are still in the silent phase of the infection. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is a key nursing duty when monitoring exposed contacts?

options.A: Performing surgical procedures in community health posts
options.B: Manufacturing vaccines for local distribution campaigns
options.C: Prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics to every contact
options.D: Monitoring exposed individuals daily for early symptom signs

explanation: Active surveillance involves regularly checking on exposed people to catch the very first signs of illness. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h7)

question: An exposed family member wants to go out because they feel fine during the incubation window. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Tell them they can go out since they lack a fever today
options.B: Discharge them from contact tracing records immediately
options.C: Administer a therapeutic dose of intravenous fluids
options.D: Explain the risk of spreading the infection before symptoms show

explanation: Patients need to know that feeling well during the incubation period does not mean they cannot develop or spread the illness. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T9#GNS313_U1_T9_h7)

question: What defines a communicable disease in a clinical setting?

options.A: A genetic disorder passed down through family generations
options.B: An illness transmitted from a reservoir to a susceptible host
options.C: A chronic condition caused by long-term environmental stress
options.D: An acute injury resulting from a physical trauma event

explanation: Communicable diseases are characterized by their ability to spread from a source to a vulnerable person. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why are regions like Nigeria often heavily impacted by communicable diseases?

options.A: Healthcare facilities completely refuse to treat infectious patients
options.B: Environmental and socio-economic factors make it easier for germs to spread
options.C: Local populations lack natural immunity to all known bacteria
options.D: Genetic mutations occur more frequently in tropical climates

explanation: Socio-economic challenges and environmental conditions often create favorable habitats for disease transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h1)

question: What are the three components of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Agent, host, and environment
options.B: Source, transmission, and cure
options.C: Pathogen, toxin, and symptom
options.D: Reservoir, vector, and portal

explanation: The epidemiological triangle models disease occurrence using the agent, host, and environment framework. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h2)

question: What happens when a single link in the chain of infection is broken?

options.A: The pathogen becomes stronger and more resistant
options.B: The transmission of the disease stops entirely
options.C: The host develops instant lifelong immunity to it
options.D: The infection changes into a non-communicable illness

explanation: Interrupted links prevent the pathogen from successfully reaching and infecting a new host. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h2)

question: What characterizes direct transmission of a communicable disease?

options.A: Carriage of infectious agents by mosquitoes and other insects
options.B: Inhalation of germs floating across an entire room
options.C: Immediate physical contact between infected and susceptible individuals
options.D: Transfer of pathogens through contaminated drinking water supplies

explanation: Direct transmission requires physical touch or close personal contact without an intermediate vehicle. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h3)

question: A patient contracts malaria after being bitten by an infected mosquito. What type of transmission is this?

options.A: Vector-borne transmission
options.B: Vehicle-borne transmission
options.C: Direct transmission
options.D: Airborne transmission

explanation: Mosquitoes act as living vectors that carry and transmit the malaria parasite to humans. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is the incubation period of a communicable disease?

options.A: Time from germ entry until the first symptoms appear
options.B: Phase when full-blown classic symptoms are clearly visible
options.C: Period marked by mild and non-specific signs of illness
options.D: Duration of recovery and tissue repair in the body

explanation: The incubation period represents the silent phase before clinical manifestations emerge. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h4)

question: Why does a poorly nourished host face a higher risk during an infection?

options.A: The incubation period becomes permanently fixed and longer
options.B: Malnutrition prevents indirect transmission of airborne agents
options.C: Pathogens multiply slower when nutrients are severely lacking
options.D: A weakened immune system makes it harder for the body to fight infections

explanation: Poor nutritional status impairs immune function, making it difficult for the body to fight off pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which vector is responsible for transmitting the malaria parasite in Nigeria?

options.A: Female Anopheles mosquito
options.B: Black fly
options.C: Aedes aegypti mosquito
options.D: Tsetse fly

explanation: The female Anopheles mosquito serves as the biological vector for malaria-causing Plasmodium species. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary mode of transmission for cholera outbreaks in communities?

options.A: Direct skin contact with infected animal reservoirs
options.B: Contaminated water and poor sanitation infrastructure
options.C: Bites from infected insect vectors during the night
options.D: Inhalation of airborne droplet nuclei in crowded rooms

explanation: Cholera is a waterborne bacterial infection typically spread through poor sanitation and unsafe drinking water. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of public health surveillance?

options.A: Manufacturing vaccines and pharmaceutical drugs for clinics
options.B: Providing direct bedside nursing care to hospitalized patients
options.C: Ongoing collection and analysis of health data for disease control
options.D: Enforcing strict quarantine laws on international travelers

explanation: Surveillance tracks disease trends to inform public health planning and intervention. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why must nurses report notifiable diseases to health authorities quickly?

options.A: To allow rapid containment and resource mobilization during outbreaks
options.B: To fulfill a legal requirement without affecting public health outcomes
options.C: To prevent the development of drug-resistant bacterial strains
options.D: To guarantee immediate financial compensation for the affected hospital

explanation: Early notification triggers timely public health responses that limit disease spread in the community. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h6)

question: Which intervention represents primary prevention of a communicable disease?

options.A: Isolating an infectious patient in a dedicated hospital ward
options.B: Providing rehabilitation therapy for chronic illness damage
options.C: Administering routine immunizations to healthy children
options.D: Screening patients for early signs of an existing infection

explanation: Primary prevention stops the disease from occurring in the first place through measures like vaccination. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h7)

question: A community nurse organizes a blood screening camp to find asymptomatic carriers of an infection. What level of prevention is this?

options.A: Tertiary prevention
options.B: Quaternary prevention
options.C: Primary prevention
options.D: Secondary prevention

explanation: Screening aims for early detection and prompt treatment, which defines secondary prevention. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T1#GNS313_U2_T1_h7)

question: In hospital infection control, Transmission-Based Precautions are considered which level of prevention?

options.A: The third tier
options.B: The final tier
options.C: The first tier
options.D: The second tier

explanation: Transmission-Based Precautions serve as the second level of infection prevention, used alongside standard precautions. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h1)

question: When should a nurse start using Transmission-Based Precautions for a patient?

options.A: At the time of patient discharge from the ward
options.B: When specific routes of pathogen transmission are suspected
options.C: During routine vital sign collection for all admissions
options.D: Only after laboratory confirmation of an infection

explanation: These precautions are applied based on clinical signs before lab results are even ready. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h1)

question: Which patients require the use of standard precautions?

options.A: Only patients with diagnosed infections
options.B: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.C: Immunocompromised individuals exclusively
options.D: All patients in healthcare settings

explanation: Standard precautions apply universally to every patient care encounter to protect against blood and body fluids. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h2)

question: A nurse touches a patient's intact skin to check pulse. What action is required under standard precautions?

options.A: Put on a plastic apron
options.B: Perform hand hygiene
options.C: Wear sterile gloves
options.D: Don a surgical mask

explanation: Touching intact skin does not require gloves, but hand hygiene must be performed before and after contact. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h2)

question: What protective items are needed when entering a room under contact precautions?

options.A: Shoe covers and gloves
options.B: A face shield and cap
options.C: A respirator and goggles
options.D: Gloves and a gown

explanation: Contact precautions require gloves and a gown to stop germs from spreading from skin or clothing. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h3)

question: A patient with a wound infection caused by a resistant bug needs vital signs checked. How should equipment be handled?

options.A: Use bare hands and wash equipment in the utility sink
options.B: Use shared ward equipment after wiping it with water
options.C: Bring all equipment from home for this specific patient
options.D: Keep dedicated equipment inside the patient room

explanation: Leaving dedicated equipment in the room prevents spreading resistant germs to other patients on the ward. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h3)

question: What is the maximum distance large respiratory droplets typically travel through the air?

options.A: Fifteen meters
options.B: Ten meters
options.C: Five meters
options.D: One meter

explanation: Large droplets quickly fall to the ground and generally do not travel further than one meter from the source. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h4)

question: Which common illness requires the nurse to use droplet precautions?

options.A: Pulmonary tuberculosis
options.B: Varicella zoster
options.C: Measles virus
options.D: Seasonal influenza

explanation: Influenza spreads via large respiratory droplets, whereas tuberculosis, chickenpox, and measles require airborne precautions. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h4)

question: What type of room airflow is needed for patients on airborne precautions?

options.A: Neutral pressure room
options.B: Positive pressure room
options.C: Standard air-conditioned room
options.D: Negative pressure room

explanation: Negative pressure stops infectious air from leaking out into the hallway when the door is opened. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h5)

question: Why is a normal surgical mask not enough when caring for a patient with pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: It restricts the nurse's vision during procedures
options.B: It absorbs too much moisture from the breath
options.C: It is too expensive for routine ward use
options.D: It allows microscopic droplet nuclei to pass through

explanation: Surgical masks do not have the tight seal needed to block tiny airborne tuberculosis bacteria. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h5)

question: When putting on personal protective equipment, which item goes on first?

options.A: Goggles
options.B: Mask
options.C: Gown
options.D: Gloves

explanation: The isolation gown is put on first to cover your clothing completely before adding other gear. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h6)

question: Which of these is an UNSAFE practice when removing personal protective equipment?

options.A: Pulling off the gown from the neck and rolling it away from the body
options.B: Performing hand hygiene between removing different PPE items
options.C: Taking off the respirator mask inside the contaminated patient room
options.D: Removing gloves before taking off the isolation gown

explanation: Respirators for airborne germs should be removed outside the patient room after closing the door to avoid breathing in leftover particles. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h6)

question: What safety step must a nurse take when cohorting two patients who have the same infection in one room?

options.A: Allow family members to share their bedding
options.B: Keep the ward doors wide open for ventilation
options.C: Ensure adequate spatial separation of at least one meter between beds
options.D: Place beds less than one meter apart without partitions

explanation: Even with cohorted patients, leaving space between beds lowers the chance of cross-infection. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h7)

question: A patient on droplet precautions needs to be taken to the radiology department for an X-ray. What must be done?

options.A: Ask radiology staff to turn off their ventilation system
options.B: Have the patient wear a surgical mask during transport
options.C: Transport the patient without any face covering
options.D: Transport the patient only during visiting hours

explanation: A surgical mask worn by the patient traps respiratory droplets while moving through public hospital areas. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h7)

question: How can a nurse manage hand hygiene during a water outage in a local Nigerian clinic?

options.A: Use improvised devices like tippy-taps with treated water and soap
options.B: Soak hands in a basin of stagnant water shared by all staff
options.C: Skip hand hygiene until running tap water is restored
options.D: Wipe hands clean with a dry cloth after every procedure

explanation: Improvised running water setups like tippy-taps offer a practical way to wash hands when piped water is unavailable. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h8)

question: What common challenge often affects infection control in primary healthcare settings in Nigeria?

options.A: Excessive supplies of disposable respirators
options.B: An overabundance of negative pressure isolation rooms
options.C: Uninterrupted power supply across all wards
options.D: Frequent water shortages and irregular PPE stocks

explanation: Clinics often face challenges with water scarcity and keeping protective gear in stock. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T10#GNS313_U2_T10_h8)

question: What defines a susceptible host in the chain of infection?

options.A: A person lacking immunity to a specific pathogen
options.B: A vector that transmits disease between humans
options.C: An individual who carries a pathogen without symptoms
options.D: An environment that supports microbial growth

explanation: A susceptible host is specifically someone who does not possess sufficient resistance or immunity to prevent an infection when exposed to a pathogen. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h1)

question: Why are elderly patients typically classified as susceptible hosts?

options.A: They experience a natural age-related decline in immune function
options.B: They have increased baseline metabolic rates
options.C: They live in isolated rural community environments
options.D: They consume higher amounts of processed food daily

explanation: Aging brings immunosenescence, which gradually weakens the body's ability to mount an effective immune response against new or latent infections. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which component provides the body's immediate, non-specific defense against pathogens?

options.A: Innate immunity
options.B: Vaccine-induced response
options.C: Antibody memory cells
options.D: Adaptive immunity

explanation: Innate immunity represents the non-specific defense mechanisms present from birth that act immediately or within hours of an antigen's appearance. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary function of adaptive immunity in the human body?

options.A: Generating targeted responses and long-lasting immunological memory
options.B: Maintaining the physical integrity of skin and mucous membranes
options.C: Triggering immediate non-specific local inflammatory reactions
options.D: Producing stomach acid to destroy ingested microorganisms

explanation: Adaptive immunity specifically targets specific antigens and creates memory cells that recognize and neutralize the pathogen rapidly during future exposures. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h2)

question: How does passive immunization protect a susceptible host?

options.A: By providing ready-made antibodies from another source
options.B: By introducing weakened live pathogens into the bloodstream
options.C: By stimulating the host to produce its own memory cells
options.D: By strengthening the physical barriers of the skin

explanation: Passive immunization introduces preformed antibodies into the body, granting immediate protection that wanes over time because the host does not manufacture them. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h3)

question: A patient receives tetanus immune globulin after stepping on a rusty nail. What type of protection does this represent?

options.A: Artificial passive immunity
options.B: Artificial active immunity
options.C: Natural active immunity
options.D: Natural passive immunity

explanation: Administering immune globulin manufactured outside the body gives artificial passive immunity, offering immediate antibody protection for an acute exposure. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h3)

question: Which mineral is commonly emphasized in community health for supporting immune function?

options.A: Zinc
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Sodium
options.D: Potassium

explanation: Zinc is vital for normal development and function of cells mediating innate immunity, neutrophils, and natural killer cells. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h4)

question: How does chronic psychological stress negatively impact a susceptible host?

options.A: It accelerates the maturation of protective T cells
options.B: Elevated cortisol suppresses lymphocyte proliferation
options.C: It increases the immediate production of antibodies
options.D: It enhances the physical barrier of mucous membranes

explanation: Sustained high levels of cortisol from chronic stress dampen immune responses by inhibiting white blood cell activity and inflammatory cytokines. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of chemoprophylaxis in public health?

options.A: Providing permanent natural immunity against viral pathogens
options.B: Curing a chronic disease that has already caused tissue damage
options.C: Replacing the function of failing adaptive immune cells
options.D: Preventing an infection from establishing in exposed individuals

explanation: Chemoprophylaxis uses medications specifically to stop a pathogen from taking hold and causing active illness after a known or suspected exposure. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h5)

question: Why must nurses carefully monitor patients taking prophylactic medications?

options.A: To confirm that passive immunity has converted into active immunity
options.B: To measure the permanent increase in patient white blood cells
options.C: To prevent misuse that can lead to antimicrobial resistance
options.D: To ensure the drug immediately stimulates active antibody production

explanation: Inappropriate or incomplete use of prophylactic drugs creates selective pressure, encouraging pathogens to develop resistance against standard treatments. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h5)

question: Which intervention represents an environmental control for vector-borne diseases?

options.A: Providing oral rehydration therapy
options.B: Using insecticide-treated bed nets
options.C: Screening blood samples for antibodies
options.D: Administering daily multivitamin supplements

explanation: Insecticide-treated bed nets modify the environment by creating a physical and chemical barrier against mosquitoes that transmit diseases like malaria. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h6)

question: Why is hand hygiene emphasized as a cornerstone behavioral modification?

options.A: It mechanically removes transient pathogens before entry
options.B: It provides long-lasting passive immunity on the skin
options.C: It stimulates the production of permanent T-cell memory
options.D: It neutralizes toxins present in contaminated drinking water

explanation: Washing hands with soap and water physically lifts and washes away microorganisms picked up from surfaces, stopping them from entering mucous membranes. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h6)

question: What is the first step a nurse takes when planning host protection in a community?

options.A: Conducting a thorough assessment of local risk factors
options.B: Administering mass active immunizations immediately
options.C: Constructing sanitary facilities for waste disposal
options.D: Distributing chemoprophylactic drugs to every household

explanation: Effective public health nursing begins with assessing specific community vulnerabilities, demographics, and disease burdens before implementing interventions. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h7)

question: A community health nurse notices low vaccine uptake in a rural settlement. What action should the nurse prioritize first?

options.A: Report the community leaders to local health authorities for negligence
options.B: Stop visiting the settlement and focus efforts on urban centers
options.C: Investigate local beliefs and barriers to provide tailored education
options.D: Begin mandatory vaccination sweeps using local law enforcement

explanation: Understanding cultural perspectives and specific barriers allows the nurse to design effective, acceptable educational strategies that improve participation. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T11#GNS313_U2_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary public health benefit of achieving high herd immunity within a community?

options.A: Reduction in the cost of treating chronic non-communicable diseases
options.B: Protection of vulnerable individuals who cannot receive vaccines
options.C: Elimination of the need for routine environmental sanitation
options.D: Complete eradication of all known bacterial pathogens globally

explanation: Herd immunity protects vulnerable people who cannot take vaccines by stopping the spread of disease in the community. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h1)

question: How does a vaccine primarily protect an individual against a specific infectious disease?

options.A: By stimulating the body's immune system to build resistance
options.B: By directly killing active pathogens circulating in the bloodstream
options.C: By coating the mucous membranes to block physical entry
options.D: By temporarily replacing the natural white blood cell count

explanation: Vaccines introduce antigens to trigger the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells for future protection. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which component of the immune system produces specific proteins to neutralize foreign antigens?

options.A: B-lymphocytes
options.B: Epithelial cells
options.C: Red blood cells
options.D: Platelets

explanation: B-lymphocytes are responsible for producing antibodies that specifically target and neutralize foreign antigens. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h2)

question: What is the primary role of memory cells created after vaccine administration?

options.A: To signal the brain to trigger a high fever response
options.B: To provide a rapid defense upon future exposure to the pathogen
options.C: To transport the vaccine contents safely out of the body
options.D: To constantly destroy normal healthy tissue in the local muscle

explanation: Memory cells remain in the body to recognize and fight off the real disease quickly if exposed later. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which type of vaccine uses a weakened, live version of the target pathogen?

options.A: Toxoid vaccine
options.B: Subunit vaccine
options.C: Live-attenuated vaccine
options.D: Inactivated vaccine

explanation: Live-attenuated vaccines contain weakened living organisms that mimic natural infection without causing severe disease. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h3)

question: Why are live-attenuated vaccines generally CONTRAINDICATED for pregnant women?

options.A: They fail to stimulate any measurable antibody response during pregnancy
options.B: The weakened organism could potentially replicate and harm the fetus
options.C: The hormones in pregnancy neutralize the live viral particles instantly
options.D: They immediately cause severe systemic anaphylactic shock in mothers

explanation: Live vaccines carry a small risk of uncontrolled replication in immunocompromised hosts, including developing fetuses. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h3)

question: Which vaccines are routinely administered to a newborn infant immediately at birth in Nigeria?

options.A: Pentavalent, PCV, and Measles vaccine
options.B: Tetanus toxoid and Yellow fever vaccine
options.C: BCG, OPV 0, and Hepatitis B birth dose
options.D: Rotavirus and Inactivated Polio Vaccine

explanation: Newborns receive BCG, OPV zero, and the Hepatitis B birth dose right after delivery to protect against early infections. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h4)

question: A mother brings her 14-week-old infant to the clinic for routine immunization. Which specific vaccines are due at this visit according to the Nigerian schedule?

options.A: BCG, Hepatitis B birth dose, and OPV 0
options.B: Pentavalent 1, PCV 1, Rotavirus, and OPV 1
options.C: Measles first dose and Yellow Fever vaccine
options.D: Pentavalent 3, PCV 3, OPV 3, and IPV

explanation: At 14 weeks, infants receive the third doses of pentavalent, PCV, and OPV, plus the Inactivated Polio Vaccine. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the recommended temperature range for storing refrigerator-sensitive vaccines like Pentavalent and PCV?

options.A: -5°C to 0°C
options.C: +2°C to +8°C

explanation: Most routine vaccines like pentavalent and PCV must be kept in standard refrigerators between +2°C and +8°C. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h5)

question: What happens to toxoid and adjuvanted vaccines if they are accidentally frozen in the cold chain?

options.A: They require dilution with warm sterile water before use
options.B: Their expiration date extends by an extra six months
options.C: Their potency is permanently destroyed and they become unsafe
options.D: They convert automatically into live-attenuated viral strains

explanation: Freezing alters the aluminum adjuvant structure in toxoid and killed vaccines, ruining their ability to stimulate immunity. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h5)

question: Where is the preferred anatomical site for giving an intramuscular vaccine to an infant under one year of age?

options.A: Deltoid muscle of the upper arm
options.B: Dorsal gluteal muscle of the buttock
options.C: Upper outer quadrant of the abdomen
options.D: Anterolateral aspect of the thigh

explanation: The anterolateral thigh muscle is well-developed in infants and avoids the risk of sciatic nerve injury. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h6)

question: Why is the BCG vaccine given strictly via the intradermal route rather than intramuscularly?

options.A: To ensure rapid systemic distribution directly into the major veins
options.B: To bypass the liver metabolism before reaching the bloodstream
options.C: To achieve slow absorption and produce a characteristic skin scar
options.D: To completely prevent any local inflammatory reaction from occurring

explanation: BCG must be given intradermally to ensure proper localized reaction and formation of the classic scar indicating immunity. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h6)

question: What type of AEFI occurs when a nurse accidentally uses an unsterile needle or incorrect diluent during vaccination?

options.A: Coincidental medical event
options.B: Vaccine quality defect-related reaction
options.C: Immunization error-related reaction
options.D: Vaccine product-related reaction

explanation: Errors in handling, preparation, or administration by staff lead directly to immunization error-related adverse events. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h7)

question: How should a nurse classify a child developing a unrelated viral malaria fever two days after receiving a routine polio vaccine?

options.A: Vaccine product-related reaction
options.B: Coincidental event
options.C: Quality defect-related reaction
options.D: Immunization anxiety-related reaction

explanation: An event that happens after vaccination by pure coincidence without causal link to the vaccine is a coincidental event. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h7)

question: What term describes the delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of vaccination services?

options.A: Vaccine hesitancy
options.B: Immunization error
options.C: Herd immunity
options.D: Cold chain failure

explanation: Vaccine hesitancy refers to reluctance or refusal to vaccinate despite available services. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h8)

question: A community health nurse encounters a mother who refuses to vaccinate her child due to rumors heard in the marketplace. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Send the mother away from the clinic immediately until she changes her mind
options.B: Listen to the mother's concerns empathetically and provide clear factual education
options.C: Ignore her concerns and quickly administer the vaccines without her consent
options.D: Threaten to report the mother to local law enforcement authorities for child neglect

explanation: Engaging parents respectfully, listening to their fears, and educating them builds trust and helps overcome hesitancy. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T12#GNS313_U2_T12_h8)

question: What primary dietary component supplies the amino acids needed to build antibodies?

options.A: Minerals
options.B: Proteins
options.C: Vitamins
options.D: Carbohydrates

explanation: Proteins break down into amino acids, which serve as the fundamental building blocks for antibodies and immune cells. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why does poor nutrition often lead to frequent illnesses in patients?

options.A: Inability to rapidly produce sufficient white blood cells
options.B: Excessive production of red blood cells blocking pathways
options.C: Rapid destruction of circulating beneficial blood platelets
options.D: Permanent damage to the outer skin barrier tissues

explanation: Immune cell proliferation requires continuous energy and nutritional substrates that are absent during dietary deficiency. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h1)

question: Which vitamin specifically maintains the mucosal surfaces of the respiratory tract?

options.A: Vitamin D
options.B: Vitamin A
options.C: Vitamin K
options.D: Vitamin B12

explanation: Vitamin A protects epithelial tissues, keeping mucosal barriers strong against invading pathogens. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h2)

question: Why is zinc particularly important for the body's immune defense?

options.A: It directly binds and kills all strains of malaria parasites in blood.
options.B: It converts simple sugars into stored energy reserves within the liver.
options.C: It supports the normal function of neutrophils and natural killer cells.
options.D: It thickens the outer layer of human skin against insect bites.

explanation: Zinc plays a direct regulatory role in activating key white blood cells responsible for destroying invaders. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h2)

question: What term describes the mutually worsening relationship between malnutrition and infection?

options.A: The metabolic exhaustion phase
options.B: The chronic inflammatory syndrome
options.C: The infection-malnutrition complex
options.D: The primary deficiency loop

explanation: This specific complex highlights how poor nutrition invites infection, which in turn deepens malnutrition. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h3)

question: A toddler being treated for severe malaria fails to gain weight despite medications. What key intervention is missing?

options.A: Complete isolation from family members to stop reinfection
options.B: Concurrent nutritional rehabilitation to repair depleted tissues
options.C: Total restriction of fluids to prevent electrolyte overload
options.D: Immediate surgical removal of the affected lymphatic tissue

explanation: Treating the infection alone fails if the underlying nutritional deficit driving vulnerability is ignored. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h3)

question: Which group experiences the highest relative demand for nutrient density due to rapid growth?

options.A: Healthy elderly males
options.B: Teenage athletes
options.C: Middle-aged working adults
options.D: Infants and young children

explanation: Rapid cell division and skeletal growth during early life require high amounts of nutrients relative to body size. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h4)

question: What is the primary reason household food insecurity impacts infants before other family members?

options.A: Infant digestive tracts cannot process local staple food crops.
options.B: Adults deliberately consume all available nutrient-dense food first.
options.C: Their high metabolic demand leaves no margin for inadequate intake.
options.D: Babies lose stored body fat faster than adults during cold nights.

explanation: Small bodies growing quickly require constant nutrient inputs, making them immediately sensitive to shortages. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h4)

question: What public health strategy involves adding missing nutrients to widely consumed commercial food items?

options.A: Biochemical farming
options.B: Therapeutic purging
options.C: Dietary restriction
options.D: Food fortification

explanation: Fortification adds micronutrients to staples like flour or oil to prevent widespread deficiencies at the population level. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h5)

question: Why is utilizing locally available foods emphasized during community nutrition education in Nigeria?

options.A: Imported nutritional supplements are entirely illegal to distribute.
options.B: Traditional cooking methods destroy all harmful food toxins.
options.C: Local food crops contain zero carbohydrates and high protein.
options.D: It ensures long-term sustainability and cultural acceptance.

explanation: Families can easily maintain dietary changes when recommended foods are locally accessible and culturally familiar. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h5)

question: Which anthropometric measurement is commonly used by community nurses to quickly screen for acute malnutrition in children?

options.A: Mid-upper arm circumference
options.B: Total body surface area
options.C: Cranial bone density index
options.D: Resting blood pressure rate

explanation: MUAC tape provides a fast, reliable indicator of muscle wasting and acute malnutrition in community settings. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h6)

question: Why is physical inspection for signs like hair thinning and skin lesions included in a nutritional assessment?

options.A: Laboratory tests are completely unreliable for detecting protein levels.
options.B: These signs prove the patient has an active bacterial blood infection.
options.C: Nutritional deficiencies manifest visible changes in rapidly dividing tissues.
options.D: Skin and hair conditions always indicate an underlying genetic disorder.

explanation: Tissues with rapid turnover, such as skin, hair, and mucosal linings, show early outward signs of nutrient shortages. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T13#GNS313_U2_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of Behavioural Change Communication in health?

options.A: Prescribing pharmaceutical medications
options.B: Shifting personal habits and social norms
options.C: Diagnosing rare tropical infections
options.D: Treating acute surgical emergencies

explanation: BCC focuses on modifying attitudes, practices, and community norms rather than merely providing medical treatment or diagnosis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h1)

question: How does BCC differ from basic health education?

options.A: BCC focuses on shifting actual practices and norms
options.B: BCC only targets medical doctors and pharmacists
options.C: Basic education is strictly for hospital inpatients
options.D: Basic education requires advanced laboratory testing

explanation: While basic education shares information, BCC actively drives lifestyle and behavioral modification among target populations. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which stage describes a person who has no intention of changing their habits?

options.A: Preparation
options.B: Maintenance
options.C: Precontemplation
options.D: Action

explanation: During precontemplation, individuals are unaware of or resistant to the idea that they need to change a habit. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h2)

question: A patient actively practices a new diet for two weeks. Which stage of change does this represent?

options.A: Maintenance
options.B: Action
options.C: Contemplation
options.D: Precontemplation

explanation: The action stage involves the direct, active implementation of the new health behavior. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h2)

question: What is the first step in designing a community-based health intervention?

options.A: Purchasing expensive medical equipment
options.B: Building a new primary health clinic
options.C: Enforcing strict state health laws
options.D: Assessing community needs and readiness

explanation: Interventions must be built upon a solid understanding of what the community actually requires and is ready to accept. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h3)

question: Why must nurses evaluate local beliefs before launching a new health campaign?

options.A: Local traditions dictate the required drug dosages
options.B: Community leaders manage all hospital finances
options.C: Ministry guidelines forbid launching unapproved programs
options.D: Fatalistic views can hinder the motivation to change

explanation: If a population believes health outcomes cannot be altered, they will lack the readiness to adopt new behaviors. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h3)

question: Who are key local stakeholders to involve when planning community health campaigns in Nigeria?

options.A: Foreign software engineers
options.B: Traditional and religious leaders
options.C: International airline pilots
options.D: Commercial construction contractors

explanation: Traditional and religious leaders hold immense influence over community attitudes and compliance with health messages. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h4)

question: A health outreach in a rural village fails because the language used was unfamiliar. What should the nurse do next?

options.A: Continue using the same pamphlets since they were approved centrally
options.B: Cancel all future health programs in that specific region permanently
options.C: Report the community members to local security forces for non-compliance
options.D: Partner with local translators and community elders to revise the message

explanation: Adapting communication to match local linguistic and cultural frameworks is essential for acceptance and trust. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h4)

question: What is a practical way for nurses to promote physical activity among community members?

options.A: Encouraging brisk walking and active daily routines
options.B: Advising patients to run marathons every weekend
options.C: Prescribing high-intensity weightlifting for the elderly
options.D: Mandating membership in expensive private fitness clubs

explanation: Practical physical activities like walking integrate easily into daily life without requiring financial resources or special equipment. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h5)

question: Which dietary advice is most appropriate for a patient managing hypertension in Nigeria?

options.A: Completely eliminating all forms of carbohydrates from every meal
options.B: Eating exclusively imported canned foods from foreign supermarkets
options.C: Consuming high amounts of processed vegetable oils daily
options.D: Focusing on affordable local whole foods and reducing salt intake

explanation: Local whole foods provide essential nutrients without the high sodium and chemical additives found in many processed options. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h5)

question: What interviewing technique helps clients explore their ambivalence regarding substance use?

options.A: Aggressive interrogation
options.B: Motivational interviewing
options.C: Strict authoritarian lecturing
options.D: Silent observation

explanation: Motivational interviewing is a collaborative, person-centered counseling style that addresses ambivalence about change. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h6)

question: Why is avoiding stigmatizing language crucial when caring for individuals with substance use disorders?

options.A: Stigma discourages patients from seeking help or returning to the clinic
options.B: Patients with addiction are unaffected by how healthcare workers speak
options.C: Stigmatizing words automatically cure physiological withdrawal symptoms
options.D: Insurance companies require polite terminology for billing purposes

explanation: Judgmental attitudes create barriers, causing vulnerable individuals to hide their struggles and avoid essential healthcare services. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h6)

question: What is the difference between monitoring and evaluation in public health?

options.A: Monitoring is done by doctors, while evaluation is done by patients
options.B: Monitoring tracks activities, while evaluation measures long-term impact
options.C: Monitoring focuses on finances, while evaluation focuses on surgery
options.D: Monitoring is unnecessary in community health nursing

explanation: Monitoring occurs during implementation to track progress, whereas evaluation assesses ultimate outcomes and effectiveness. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h7)

question: Which factor represents a major structural barrier to exclusive breastfeeding among market women?

options.A: Excessive availability of free infant formula in clinics
options.B: Complete absence of infants in rural Nigerian communities
options.C: A sudden lack of interest in infant nutrition education
options.D: Economic pressure to return immediately to informal trading

explanation: Financial survival needs often force mothers to resume work quickly, making exclusive breastfeeding challenging without supportive environments. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T14#GNS313_U2_T14_h7)

question: What primary body system does the poliovirus target?

options.A: Respiratory system
options.B: Circulatory system
options.C: Nervous system
options.D: Digestive system

explanation: The poliovirus specifically invades nervous tissue, which can lead to muscle weakness and paralysis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T15#GNS313_U2_T15_h1)

question: How does the poliovirus typically enter the human body?

options.A: By airborne droplets
options.B: Through the mouth
options.C: Via broken skin
options.D: Through insect bites

explanation: Transmission occurs primarily via the fecal-oral route, meaning the virus enters through the oral cavity from contaminated sources. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T15#GNS313_U2_T15_h1)

question: How many wild poliovirus strains exist?

options.A: Ten strains
options.B: One strain
options.C: Five strains
options.D: Three strains

explanation: There are three distinct wild poliovirus strains, designated as types 1, 2, and 3. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T15#GNS313_U2_T15_h2)

question: Why is human-to-human transmission essential for the survival of the poliovirus?

options.A: The virus cannot survive outside a living human cell for seconds
