explanation: Spot on! Scans can strongly suggest cancer, but a pathologist needs to look at an actual tissue sample under a microscope to confirm it. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h4)

question: What is the main goal of using the TNM staging system for lung cancer?

options.A: To determine the extent of disease spread and plan appropriate treatment
options.B: To measure the exact volume of air the lungs can hold
options.C: To calculate the patient's exact daily calorie requirements
options.D: To identify which specific type of cigarette the patient smoked

explanation: Brilliant! TNM helps the team figure out how big the tumor is, if it has reached lymph nodes, and how far it has spread, guiding the best treatment plan. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h4)

question: What is the main goal when a patient is caught early with non-small cell lung cancer?

options.A: Total lung transplantation
options.B: Surgical resection
options.C: Palliative hospice care
options.D: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy

explanation: You're doing great! If the cancer is caught early and hasn't spread, cutting out the tumor surgically gives the best chance for a complete cure. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h5)

question: How does immunotherapy work differently from standard chemotherapy?

options.A: It completely replaces the need for any diagnostic imaging procedures.
options.B: It only acts on the outer layer of the skin and never reaches the lungs.
options.C: It freezes the tumor tissue by lowering the core body temperature.
options.D: It empowers the body's own immune defenses to target and destroy cancer cells.

explanation: Exactly right! Instead of just attacking cells directly like chemo, immunotherapy helps your own white blood cells recognize and fight off the cancer. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h5)

question: As a nurse, what is the quickest way to help a patient who is suddenly struggling to catch their breath due to lung cancer?

options.A: Laying the patient flat on their back in bed
options.B: Placing the patient in a high-Fowler's position
options.C: Encouraging rapid, shallow mouth breathing
options.D: Restricting all fluid intake for twelve hours

explanation: Spot on, nurse! Sitting the patient upright in a high-Fowler's position lets their chest expand fully, making it much easier to draw breath. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h6)

question: A patient who just had lung surgery is scared to cough because their incision hurts. What should you, the nurse, do first?

options.A: Tell the patient that coughing is optional and let them sleep all day.
options.B: Apply a tight chest binder to completely immobilize the chest wall.
options.C: Administer prescribed pain medication before encouraging controlled coughing exercises.
options.D: Report the patient immediately to the surgeon for emergency re-operation.

explanation: Wonderful clinical judgment! Controlling the pain first allows the patient to cough and clear their lungs safely without agony, preventing complications like collapsed lung areas. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h6)

question: Which screening tool is best for catching lung cancer early in high-risk people who don't have symptoms yet?

options.A: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.B: Standard routine sputum culture
options.C: Pulmonary spirometry test
options.D: Low-dose computed tomography scan

explanation: You've got this! A low-dose CT scan captures clear images of the lungs using very low radiation, making it the gold standard for high-risk screening. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h7)

question: Why is quitting smoking considered 'primary prevention' rather than 'secondary prevention'?

options.A: It is only performed after a patient receives a confirmed cancer diagnosis.
options.B: It relies entirely on surgical removal of damaged bronchial tissue.
options.C: It focuses on finding small tumors before symptoms appear.
options.D: It aims to prevent the disease from ever developing in the first place.

explanation: Brilliant! Primary prevention stops harmful exposures (like tobacco) so the disease process never even gets a chance to start. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T11#GNS313_U3_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary reason public health nurses classify accidents as preventable events?

options.A: They happen exclusively due to sudden genetic health conditions
options.B: They stem from interactions between environments and human behavior
options.C: They only occur in industrial and high-risk factory zones
options.D: They are caused strictly by unavoidable natural weather phenomena

explanation: Because accidents result from physical surroundings and human actions, modifying these factors can prevent them from happening. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h1)

question: How does viewing accidents as preventable alter the approach of a community health nurse?

options.A: It eliminates the need to keep emergency trauma supplies in local clinics
options.B: It places total legal blame on the victim for every sustained injury
options.C: It stops nurses from teaching basic first aid procedures to villagers
options.D: It shifts the primary focus from treatment toward proactive safety promotion

explanation: Recognizing preventability leads nurses to focus on hazard reduction and education rather than just managing injuries after they occur. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h1)

question: Which demographic group is most vulnerable to domestic burns and scalds inside Nigerian homes?

options.A: Middle-aged office administrators
options.B: Toddlers and the elderly
options.C: Young adult commercial drivers
options.D: Adolescent school children

explanation: Young children and older adults spend more time at home and face higher risks from open fires and boiling water. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h2)

question: What is a major contributing factor to occupational injuries in Nigeria's informal work sectors?

options.A: Excessive availability of advanced medical insurance
options.B: Mandatory adherence to strict international safety laws
options.C: Lack of proper personal protective equipment usage
options.D: Overly frequent routine government factory inspections

explanation: Unorganized sectors often lack safety gear and enforcement, leading to higher rates of machinery and construction injuries. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h2)

question: An open and uncovered drainage channel in an urban Nigerian street represents which type of accident risk factor?

options.A: Physiological fatigue
options.B: Environmental hazard
options.C: Behavioral error
options.D: Genetic predisposition

explanation: Uncovered drainage systems are physical conditions in the surroundings that pose a direct danger to passersby. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h3)

question: How does poverty indirectly increase the risk of domestic accidents in urban communities?

options.A: By compelling residents to install advanced fire alarms
options.B: By forcing families into overcrowded housing with exposed wiring
options.C: By ensuring all homes have well-maintained paved pathways
options.D: By providing excessive funds for purchasing dangerous machinery

explanation: Poverty often limits housing choices, leading people to live in substandard spaces with faulty electrical setups and unsafe cooking spaces. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h3)

question: What is a common psychological consequence experienced by survivors of severe traumatic accidents?

options.A: Increased sensory perception
options.B: Post-traumatic stress disorder
options.C: Enhanced memory retention
options.D: Elevated tolerance to pain

explanation: Survivors frequently experience lasting psychological trauma like anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress following a violent accident. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h4)

question: How do widespread road traffic accidents impact the broader Nigerian healthcare system?

options.A: By decreasing the workload of orthopedic and surgical personnel
options.B: By placing a heavy financial and resource strain on emergency wards
options.C: By reducing the overall demand for outpatient pharmacy services
options.D: By providing excess funding and modern equipment to rural clinics

explanation: Sudden influxes of trauma patients overwhelm emergency departments, depleting blood supplies, medications, and staff time. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h4)

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the emergency ABCDE assessment protocol for accident victims?

options.A: Bandage
options.B: Bone
options.C: Breathing
options.D: Bleeding

explanation: In emergency trauma care, 'B' stands for assessing and managing the patient's breathing and chest movement. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h5)

question: A nurse arrives at a road crash scene and finds an unresponsive victim bleeding heavily from the leg. What is the immediate priority action?

options.A: Complete a full family medical history questionnaire on the spot
options.B: Control the major external bleeding using direct pressure
options.C: Ask the bystanders for the victim's residential home address
options.D: Perform a detailed neurological reflex examination immediately

explanation: Circulation and stopping severe hemorrhage take precedence to prevent fatal blood loss before checking other details. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h5)

question: Why is regular patient repositioning an essential nursing intervention during long-term accident recovery?

options.A: To prevent the development of pressure ulcers
options.B: To eliminate the need for any prescribed pain medication
options.C: To permanently increase the patient's resting heart rate
options.D: To accelerate the natural growth of new bone tissue

explanation: Immobilized patients are prone to skin breakdown, making frequent turning crucial to relieve pressure points. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of involving physical therapists in the rehabilitation phase of an injured person?

options.A: To investigate the legal liability and cause of the collision
options.B: To help restore functional mobility and physical independence
options.C: To manage the hospital billing and insurance documentation
options.D: To prescribe strong surgical antibiotics for open wound infections

explanation: Physical therapy helps patients rebuild strength, coordination, and movement skills needed for daily living. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h6)

question: Where is a community health nurse most likely to conduct outreach to reach commercial motorcyclists regarding safety?

options.A: Motor parks
options.B: Surgical wards
options.C: Pharmacy stores
options.D: Radiology clinics

explanation: Motor parks are gathering hubs for commercial transport workers, making them ideal locations for targeted safety education. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h7)

question: Why should community health nurses collaborate with local leaders when planning accident prevention programs?

options.A: To transfer all nursing clinical responsibilities to political figures
options.B: To secure direct permission to prescribe emergency surgical drugs
options.C: To bypass the need for conducting any public health lectures
options.D: To ensure better community participation and enforcement of safety habits

explanation: Local leaders hold influence over community members, helping to drive acceptance and adherence to safety guidelines. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T12#GNS313_U3_T12_h7)

question: In basic terms, what is a poison?

options.A: Any substance that disrupts body functions or causes harm when introduced
options.B: A prescription drug taken strictly according to doctor instructions
options.C: A chemical compound that only harms the liver and kidneys
options.D: An infectious microorganism found in contaminated water sources

explanation: Spot on! A poison is simply anything that enters the body and causes harm or upsets normal body functions. You've got this! [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h1)

question: Why are toddlers so prone to accidental poisoning at home?

options.A: Their natural curiosity drives them to taste and explore colorful items
options.B: Parents frequently leave dangerous medications inside school bags
options.C: Toddlers are usually employed to handle agricultural pesticides
options.D: They possess a high genetic tolerance for household chemicals

explanation: Exactly! Little ones love to explore everything using their mouths, often mistaking bright chemicals or syrups for sweet treats. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h1)

question: In Nigerian homes, which household liquid is most often accidentally swallowed by children because it's stored in empty drink bottles?

options.A: Clean water
options.B: Cooking oil
options.C: Fruit juice
options.D: Kerosene

explanation: Well done! Storing kerosene in old soft drink bottles is a major hazard because kids easily mistake it for water or juice. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h2)

question: What makes farming pesticides particularly dangerous in rural areas?

options.A: Farmers use them exclusively as food flavoring agents in local dishes
options.B: They are frequently stored near food items and handled without protective gear
options.C: They only affect animals and have zero toxic impact on human physiology
options.D: They lose their toxicity completely within a few minutes of application

explanation: Spot on! When chemicals are kept close to food and used without gloves or masks, accidental poisoning happens easily. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h2)

question: Through which route do gases or vapors enter the bloodstream the fastest?

options.A: Inhalation
options.B: Subcutaneous contact
options.C: Ingestion
options.D: Skin absorption

explanation: You got it! Breathing in a gas sends it straight through the huge surface area of the lungs directly into the blood. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h3)

question: How do organophosphate poisons mess with the nervous system?

options.A: By blocking acetylcholinesterase and causing neurotransmitter accumulation
options.B: By drying up all bodily fluids through immediate kidney failure
options.C: By turning the blood acidic within seconds of skin contact
options.D: By freezing the spinal cord to completely stop all nerve impulses

explanation: That's right! They block the enzyme that normally cleans up acetylcholine, meaning nerves keep firing continuously without a break. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h3)

question: Which sign is a classic giveaway of an opioid overdose?

options.A: Pinpoint pupils
options.B: Extreme pupil dilation
options.C: Uncontrollable muscle tremors
options.D: Severe skin redness and sweating

explanation: Spot on! Tiny, pinpoint pupils combined with slow breathing are classic red flags for opioid overdose. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h4)

question: A farmer arrives at the clinic drooling, tearing up, peeing frequently, and having muscle twitches after spraying the farm. What is this?

options.A: Sedative overdose from sleeping pills
options.B: Cholinergic poisoning from organophosphates
options.C: Caustic poisoning from swallowed acid
options.D: Opioid poisoning from strong painkillers

explanation: Correct! Remember the DUMBELS sign (drooling, urination, muscle twitching, etc.)—it points straight to organophosphate poisoning. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h4)

question: Why should you NEVER make a patient vomit after they swallow kerosene?

options.A: It makes the poison taste much worse on its way back up
options.B: It can cause the chemical to enter the lungs and cause aspiration pneumonia
options.C: It immediately neutralizes all medications given in the hospital
options.D: It causes instant blindness in both eyes

explanation: Well done! Coming back up, kerosene can easily slip into the windpipe and lungs, causing severe chemical pneumonia. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h5)

question: What is the immediate nursing action if a chemical splashes into a patient's eyes?

options.A: Wait for laboratory blood test results before touching the face
options.B: Cover the eyes tightly with dry gauze bandages without washing
options.C: Flush the eyes continuously with clean water for at least fifteen minutes
options.D: Apply concentrated acid neutralizer drops directly to the corneas

explanation: Spot on! Quick and long flushing with clean water washes the chemical away before it can permanently damage the cornea. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h5)

question: What is the best way to prevent accidental poisoning in community health?

options.A: Building specialized intensive care units in every village clinic
options.B: Educating families on proper chemical storage and prohibiting food-container reuse
options.C: Training traditional healers to perform emergency gastric lavage
options.D: Banning the sale of all cleaning agents and agricultural chemicals

explanation: Correct! Teaching families how to safely store items and never use old drink bottles for chemicals stops poisonings before they happen. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h6)

question: Which of these is a WRONG practice when it comes to preventing poisoning?

options.A: Using clear labeling on all containers holding hazardous substances
options.B: Storing kerosene and bleach in empty soft drink bottles in the kitchen
options.C: Consulting qualified health workers before taking herbal concoctions
options.D: Keeping all pharmaceutical drugs locked up away from children

explanation: You got it! Putting dangerous chemicals in drink bottles is a recipe for disaster. Always keep them in their original, clearly labeled containers. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T13#GNS313_U3_T13_h6)

question: What includes power dynamics and verbal threats in the modern definition of violence?

options.A: The focus exclusively on financial loss
options.B: The restriction to only domestic settings
options.C: The inclusion of power dynamics and verbal threats
options.D: The exclusion of psychological harm

explanation: Modern definitions of violence incorporate threatened force, power dynamics, and psychological harm alongside actual physical injury. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h1)

question: A patient has no physical wounds but reports constant intimidation and control by a spouse. What category does this fit?

options.A: Accidental injury caused by environmental hazards
options.B: Purely economic distress without health implications
options.C: Actual violence involving power and threatened force
options.D: Normal domestic disagreement requiring no intervention

explanation: Intimidation and coercive control fall under the recognized definition of threatened force and psychological abuse. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h1)

question: What is the main term for violence committed by armed groups for political goals?

options.A: Domestic violence
options.B: Collective violence
options.C: Interpersonal violence
options.D: Self-directed violence

explanation: Collective violence describes the use of force by organized groups or states to achieve political, social, or economic goals. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h2)

question: A street fight between rival groups belongs to which classification of violence?

options.A: Collective state violence
options.B: Occupational hazard
options.C: Interpersonal community violence
options.D: Self-directed abuse

explanation: Community violence between individuals or groups unrelated to each other falls under interpersonal violence. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h2)

question: Which substance frequently acts as a trigger by lowering self-control during violent incidents?

options.A: Alcohol
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Vitamins
options.D: Antibiotics

explanation: Alcohol and substance use are well-documented risk factors that lower impulse control and escalate interpersonal conflict. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h3)

question: Why does exposure to violence during childhood increase a person's vulnerability to violent situations later in life?

options.A: It permanently alters physical bone density
options.B: It guarantees lifelong employment challenges
options.C: It normalizes aggressive behaviors as standard conflict resolution
options.D: It eliminates all neurological stress responses

explanation: Witnessing or experiencing violence early in life often normalizes abuse and disrupts healthy coping mechanisms, elevating future risk. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h3)

question: What mental health condition is most commonly seen in survivors of severe trauma?

options.A: Schizoaffective disorder
options.B: Obsessive compulsive disorder
options.C: Bipolar depression
options.D: Post-traumatic stress disorder

explanation: Post-traumatic stress disorder is a common psychological consequence experienced by survivors of intense physical or emotional violence. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h4)

question: How does widespread community violence affect local healthcare delivery?

options.A: It reduces overall patient admissions
options.B: It improves community sanitation standards
options.C: It increases medical equipment donations
options.D: It strains medical facilities and disrupts service accessibility

explanation: High levels of violence overwhelm emergency infrastructure and often force healthcare workers or facilities to curtail operations. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h4)

question: Why do many victims of violence hide the true cause of their injuries from nurses?

options.A: Fear, shame, or threats from perpetrators
options.B: Desire to pay higher hospital bills
options.C: Preference for surgical procedures
options.D: Lack of physical pain

explanation: Victims frequently hide abuse out of fear of retaliation, social stigma, or emotional intimidation by the abuser. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h5)

question: What is the best way to document statements made by a patient who reports an assault?

options.A: Omit patient statements to save charting time
options.B: Summarize the story using personal medical opinions
options.C: Record exact patient statements in quotation marks
options.D: Rewrite the account using dramatic descriptions

explanation: Using direct quotes preserves factual integrity and provides legally sound documentation for potential review. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h5)

question: What principle must guide nursing care for survivors of violence?

options.A: Trauma-informed care
options.B: Financial auditing
options.C: Aggressive interrogation
options.D: Punitive deterrence

explanation: Trauma-informed care ensures that interventions avoid re-traumatizing the patient and prioritize safety, trust, and empowerment. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h6)

question: Why is a confidential safety plan important for a patient returning home after experiencing abuse?

options.A: It prevents the abuser from ever returning
options.B: It outlines actionable steps to escape acute danger
options.C: It cures post-traumatic stress disorder instantly
options.D: It guarantees financial independence

explanation: A safety plan prepares the survivor with practical strategies and emergency contacts should violence escalate again. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h6)

question: Which level of prevention focuses on community education to stop violence before it starts?

options.A: Primary prevention
options.B: Quaternary prevention
options.C: Tertiary prevention
options.D: Secondary prevention

explanation: Primary prevention aims to prevent violence entirely through educational outreach and community-wide risk reduction before abuse occurs. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h7)

question: Why is teamwork across different sectors necessary for effective violence reduction?

options.A: Police officers can perform surgical operations
options.B: Violence stems from complex social, legal, and health roots
options.C: Nurses lack basic clinical assessment skills
options.D: Hospitals possess all available community resources

explanation: Addressing the root causes of violence demands coordinated efforts across law enforcement, social services, and healthcare sectors. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T14#GNS313_U3_T14_h7)

question: What does a "double burden of disease" mean in Nigerian public health?

options.A: Having high rates of both maternal and child mortality simultaneously
options.B: Suffering from simultaneous outbreaks of waterborne and airborne infections
options.C: Managing high patient loads in both rural clinics and urban teaching hospitals
options.D: Dealing with both infectious diseases and chronic non-communicable diseases

explanation: Great job! A double burden simply means our healthcare system has to fight old enemies like malaria and TB while also managing the rising wave of lifestyle diseases like hypertension and diabetes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h1)

question: Why do non-communicable diseases (NCDs) like hypertension often go unnoticed for years?

options.A: Symptoms only appear after a person reaches retirement age
options.B: They develop silently in the body without immediate noticeable symptoms
options.C: Standard diagnostic laboratory tests cannot detect chronic illnesses early
options.D: Patients refuse to visit primary health centres for routine check-ups

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like high blood pressure creep up slowly without causing obvious pain or distress. That's why routine checks are so important for your patients. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h1)

question: How is Behavioural Change Communication (BCC) different from basic health education?

options.A: Basic health education focuses exclusively on preventing infectious diseases
options.B: BCC is only used inside hospital wards by qualified physicians and nurse specialists
options.C: BCC uses interactive dialogue and addresses social obstacles rather than just giving facts
options.D: Basic health education relies heavily on mass media television broadcasts

explanation: You've got it! While basic education just tells people what to do, BCC actually talks *with* them to figure out what's stopping them from living healthier lives. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h2)

question: A nurse wants to address high salt intake in a local market. What should be the very first step?

options.A: Engage market vendors in a discussion about how they view salt use in local foods
options.B: Ban the sale of heavily salted processed snacks within the market stalls
options.C: Organize a mandatory lecture hall seminar for all registered market traders
options.D: Distribute brightly coloured pamphlets detailing the dangers of hypertension

explanation: Brilliant! True nursing care starts with listening. Always involve the community and understand their perspective before trying to change their habits. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h2)

question: According to the Health Belief Model, what must a patient believe first before they will change a health habit?

options.A: The government has implemented strict laws banning unhealthy food imports
options.B: Their local primary healthcare clinic is fully funded and well-equipped
options.C: Their family members have already suffered from the same chronic illness
options.D: They are personally vulnerable to the health condition and see benefits in changing

explanation: Correct! Patients won't change unless they genuinely believe "this can happen to me" and that taking action will actually make a difference for them. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h3)

question: Why is knowing the stages of the Transtheoretical Model useful for a clinical nurse?

options.A: It accurately predicts the exact day a patient will stop smoking or exercising
options.B: It helps tailor counselling to match the patient's exact readiness to change
options.C: It proves whether a patient has a genetic predisposition to chronic illness
options.D: It replaces the need for physical assessments during routine clinic visits

explanation: Exactly right! People change at their own pace. Knowing their stage helps you meet them where they are instead of pushing too hard too fast. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h3)

question: What is the main goal of conducting a community risk factor assessment for NCDs?

options.A: To penalize local food vendors who sell cheap processed carbohydrate meals
options.B: To secure international funding grants for building specialized cardiac hospitals
options.C: To gather local data and identify specific health needs before planning interventions
options.D: To diagnose individual patients with hypertension during routine house calls

explanation: Spot on! You can't solve a problem until you understand it. Assessing the community helps you design programs that actually fit their real-life struggles. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h4)

question: Why should nurses avoid applying urban health assumptions directly to rural farming communities in Nigeria?

options.A: Rural and urban populations often have very different physical activity levels and dietary realities
options.B: Medical diagnostic equipment is completely unavailable outside major state capitals
options.C: Rural communities are completely immune to lifestyle-related chronic health conditions
options.D: Urban residents never participate in focus group discussions or health interviews

explanation: You nailed it! City life and village life are completely different. What works for an office worker in Lagos might make zero sense for a farmer in a rural community. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h4)

question: Which strategy works best when designing health messages for communities with low literacy levels?

options.A: Using pictorial guides, local radio jingles, and interactive drama performances
options.B: Relying entirely on detailed medical charts during community lectures
options.C: Distributing dense academic textbooks written in English about chronic diseases
options.D: Requiring all participants to read online health blogs before clinic visits

explanation: Wonderful! Pictures, local drama, and radio bypass reading barriers, making health education fun and easy for everyone to understand. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h5)

question: A community links weight gain with high social status, making residents resistant to weight-loss advice. What is the best nursing approach?

options.A: Reframing the message around maintaining physical strength and caring for grandchildren
options.B: Stopping health education entirely until local cultural traditions change
options.C: Focusing solely on prescription weight-loss medications available at the pharmacy
options.D: Telling them bluntly that their cultural beliefs are outdated and dangerous

explanation: Smart nursing! Good community nurses respect local culture while gently connecting healthy habits to things the people already care about deeply, like family. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h5)

question: Why is interpersonal communication considered the gold standard for changing health behaviour?

options.A: It reaches thousands of people simultaneously across multiple states
options.B: It allows for direct feedback, personal questions, and tailored guidance
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for community health workers
options.D: It costs significantly less money than printing mass media flyers

explanation: Correct! Nothing beats a real conversation. One-on-one time gives patients the chance to voice their fears and get advice built just for them. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h6)

question: What is the biggest advantage of using local community radio stations for NCD health campaigns?

options.A: They replace the need for physical clinical screening examinations
options.B: They can broadcast messages in indigenous languages to reach remote areas
options.C: They are exclusively funded by international public health organizations
options.D: They guarantee that every listener will immediately adopt a healthy diet

explanation: Spot on! Radio bridges the gap, bringing vital health messages right into homes and farms using the local dialects people speak every day. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h6)

question: What common economic challenge often forces families to rely heavily on cheap, refined carbohydrate meals?

options.A: A total lack of agricultural land for farming throughout the entire country
options.B: Financial poverty that makes fresh vegetables and lean proteins expensive
options.C: Universal free distribution of processed foods at primary healthcare centres
options.D: Strict government bans on importing nutritious food items into local markets

explanation: You've got it. Economic reality plays a huge role in health. When fresh protein and veggies are pricey, families naturally turn to cheaper, filling carbs. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h7)

question: A patient tells you they are too busy with work and transport to visit the gym. What is your best response as a nurse?

options.A: Tell them that exercise is optional if they take their blood pressure medication
options.B: Advise them to stop working so hard and prioritize leisure time instead
options.C: Suggest simple physical activities that can be built directly into daily chores and routines
options.D: Insist that they must find time for a structured gym membership every evening

explanation: Brilliant! Health advice has to be practical. Recommending things like walking more or active housework fits right into their busy schedules without costing extra money. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h7)

question: What does "process monitoring" evaluate during a community health campaign?

options.A: The exact financial profit generated by local primary health clinics
options.B: Long-term genetic changes in the community's disease risk profile
options.C: The total number of hospital beds required for severe stroke patients
options.D: Day-to-day activities like attendance numbers and media broadcasts

explanation: Correct! Process monitoring is just checking your daily checklist: Are the workshops running? Are people showing up? Did the radio jingle play? [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h8)

question: Why is long-term sustainability such an important goal for community health programs?

options.A: It guarantees that nurses will receive permanent salary increases from the state
options.B: It ensures health promotion continues after external project funding eventually stops
options.C: It prevents infectious disease outbreaks from occurring in urban slums
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for future community health assessments

explanation: Spot on! External grants and projects eventually end. Building local community leadership ensures that the good work keeps going long after outsiders leave. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T15#GNS313_U3_T15_h8)

question: What does the top number in a blood pressure reading represent?

options.A: Venous pressure
options.B: Capillary pressure
options.C: Systolic pressure
options.D: Diastolic pressure

explanation: The top number measures the pressure in the arteries when the heart contracts, known as systolic pressure. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is a single high blood pressure reading insufficient for a diagnosis of hypertension?

options.A: Doctors must always perform an ECG first
options.B: Manometers are notoriously inaccurate on first use
options.C: Temporary factors can artificially elevate readings
options.D: Normal blood pressure fluctuates very little daily

explanation: Anxiety, recent activity, or pain can cause temporary spikes, requiring repeated measurements for confirmation. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is hypertension frequently called the silent killer?

options.A: Patients refuse to talk about their diagnosis
options.B: It causes sudden death during sleep without warning
options.C: It develops without noticeable symptoms for years
options.D: Standard sphygmomanometers fail to detect it early

explanation: The condition often progresses silently without physical warning signs until major damage occurs. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h2)

question: What lifestyle shift heavily contributes to rising hypertension rates in Nigerian urban areas?

options.A: Decreased access to modern pharmaceutical drugs
options.B: Adoption of processed, high-sodium diets
options.C: Increased consumption of fresh local vegetables
options.D: Frequent participation in strenuous manual labor

explanation: Urbanization often introduces dietary habits rich in sodium and low in fresh produce, increasing vascular strain. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is the primary difference between essential and secondary hypertension?

options.A: Essential only affects individuals over sixty years
options.B: Essential develops rapidly within a few days
options.C: Secondary has a known underlying medical cause
options.D: Secondary is completely resistant to all medications

explanation: Secondary hypertension is triggered by an identifiable condition like kidney disease, unlike essential hypertension. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h3)

question: A patient presents with a family history of stroke, obesity, and high sodium intake. Which of these is a modifiable risk factor?

options.A: High sodium intake
options.B: Family history of stroke
options.C: Advanced age
options.D: Genetic predisposition

explanation: Dietary habits can be changed through patient education and behavioral modification, unlike genetics or age. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h3)

question: What blood pressure reading classifies a patient as having Stage 2 hypertension?

options.A: 140/90 mmHg or higher
options.B: Less than 120/80 mmHg

explanation: Stage 2 hypertension is clinically defined by a systolic reading of 140 or higher, or a diastolic reading of 90 or higher. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h4)

question: How should a nurse classify a patient with a systolic reading of 135 mmHg and a diastolic reading of 82 mmHg?

options.A: Stage 2 Hypertension
options.B: Normal blood pressure
options.C: Stage 1 Hypertension
options.D: Elevated blood pressure

explanation: When readings cross categories, the higher category applies; a systolic of 135 falls into Stage 1. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h4)

question: What common symptom do some patients report during the early stages of elevated blood pressure?

options.A: Complete loss of peripheral vision
options.B: Severe pain in the lower legs
options.C: Morning occipital headaches
options.D: Sudden swelling of both ankles

explanation: Early morning headaches located at the back of the head are a classic, though inconsistent, warning sign. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h5)

question: What error occurs when a nurse uses a blood pressure cuff that is too small for a patient's arm?

options.A: It has no impact on measurement accuracy
options.B: The reading will be falsely lowered
options.C: The mercury column will not rise at all
options.D: The reading will be falsely elevated

explanation: A narrow bladder requires more pressure to compress the brachial artery, resulting in an artificially high reading. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is a common side effect associated with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors?

options.A: Severe muscle weakness
options.B: Uncontrolled tremors
options.C: Persistent dry cough
options.D: Yellowing of the sclera

explanation: ACE inhibitors frequently trigger a nagging, dry cough due to the accumulation of bradykinin in the respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h6)

question: A newly diagnosed hypertensive patient is advised to reduce sodium intake. What is the primary physiological rationale for this recommendation?

options.A: Stimulates immediate vasodilation in peripheral veins
options.B: Decreases fluid retention and blood volume
options.C: Directly strengthens the left ventricular wall
options.D: Prevents the breakdown of potassium in the kidneys

explanation: High sodium pulls water into the bloodstream, increasing total fluid volume and vascular resistance. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h6)

question: What distinguishes a hypertensive emergency from a hypertensive urgency?

options.A: Absolute value of the systolic reading
options.B: Response to oral medication doses
options.C: The patient's age and medical history
options.D: Presence of acute end-organ damage

explanation: An emergency involves acute, ongoing damage to vital organs like the brain or kidneys, requiring immediate intravenous intervention. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a classic long-term complication of chronic uncontrolled hypertension?

options.A: Cerebrovascular accident
options.B: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
options.C: Chronic kidney disease
options.D: Hypertensive retinopathy

explanation: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune endocrine disorder, whereas the others are direct vascular consequences of chronic hypertension. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h7)

question: Why must community health nurses actively target public spaces like markets and churches for screening?

options.A: Many individuals do not visit formal health facilities regularly
options.B: Ministry of health mandates mobile clinics in commercial areas
options.C: People only experience high blood pressure in public settings
options.D: Static clinics lack basic equipment like stethoscopes

explanation: Taking screening services directly to the community catches undiagnosed cases in people who avoid routine hospital check-ups. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h8)

question: A patient stops taking antihypertensive drugs because they feel fine and have no headaches. How should the community nurse address this?

options.A: Suggest switching immediately to traditional herbal remedies without medical supervision
options.B: Explain that hypertension is a chronic condition that remains controlled due to the medication
options.C: Instruct the patient to double the dosage whenever a mild headache occurs
options.D: Agree that medication is unnecessary since physical symptoms have completely resolved

explanation: Patients often confuse feeling well with being cured; nurses must clarify that the drugs are maintaining normal pressure. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T2#GNS313_U3_T2_h8)

question: What is the primary physiological defect in diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Excessive insulin production
options.B: Persistent hyperglycemia
options.C: Decreased renal blood flow
options.D: Rapid glucose elimination

explanation: Diabetes mellitus is characterized primarily by chronic high blood sugar levels resulting from problems with insulin. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h1)

question: The main function of insulin in the human body is to...

options.A: allow body cells to absorb glucose
options.B: stimulate the liver to produce more sugar
options.C: destroy excess red blood cells
options.D: prevent the kidneys from filtering water

explanation: Insulin acts as a key that unlocks body cells so glucose from the bloodstream can enter and be used for energy. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h1)

question: Cellular insulin resistance means that target tissues...

options.A: destroy the pancreas directly
options.B: fail to respond properly to insulin
options.C: stop producing glucose entirely
options.D: absorb too much sugar too fast

explanation: Insulin resistance occurs when cells do not respond effectively to the hormone, preventing normal glucose uptake. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h2)

question: Which organ is responsible for producing the hormone insulin?

options.A: Pancreas
options.B: Liver
options.C: Stomach
options.D: Kidneys

explanation: Specialized beta cells within the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas synthesize and secrete insulin. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h2)

question: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is fundamentally caused by...

options.A: temporary pregnancy hormones
options.B: severe dietary sugar overload
options.C: age-related cellular wear and tear
options.D: autoimmune destruction of beta cells

explanation: Type 1 diabetes involves an immune-mediated destruction of the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h3)

question: Gestational diabetes mellitus is defined as glucose intolerance that begins...

options.A: after menopause
options.B: during pregnancy
options.C: in early childhood
options.D: following physical trauma

explanation: Gestational diabetes specifically refers to high blood sugar that is first detected during pregnancy. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h3)

question: Urbanization contributes to rising diabetes rates in Nigeria primarily through...

options.A: mandatory consumption of synthetic insulin
options.B: shifts toward processed diets and physical inactivity
options.C: reduced access to traditional medical herbs
options.D: genetic mutations caused by factory pollution

explanation: Urban lifestyle changes often involve eating more calorie-dense foods and moving less, which triggers metabolic disease. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which factor is NOT a typical lifestyle risk factor for Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Central body obesity
options.B: Regular physical exercise
options.C: Poor dietary choices
options.D: Chronic psychological stress

explanation: Regular physical exercise protects against diabetes rather than acting as a risk factor. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h4)

question: What is the medical term for excessive thirst experienced by diabetic patients?

options.A: Polydipsia
options.B: Proteinuria
options.C: Polyphagia
options.D: Polyuria

explanation: Polydipsia refers to the excessive thirst caused by fluid loss from high blood sugar levels. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h5)

question: A fasting plasma glucose test result of 7.0 mmol/L or higher indicates...

options.A: normal metabolic function
options.B: isolated renal failure
options.C: provisional diabetes mellitus
options.D: severe hypoglycemia

explanation: A fasting plasma glucose level at or above 7.0 mmol/L meets the diagnostic threshold for diabetes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h5)

question: A patient taking insulin reports feeling shaky, sweaty, and dizzy. What is the immediate nursing action?

options.A: Withhold all oral fluids and prepare for immediate surgery
options.B: Instruct the patient to exercise vigorously to burn off sugar
options.C: Check the blood glucose level and provide fast-acting carbohydrates
options.D: Administer a scheduled dose of long-acting insulin

explanation: Shakiness and sweating indicate hypoglycemia, which requires immediate confirmation and treatment with fast-acting sugar. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h6)

question: Why is rotating subcutaneous insulin injection sites clinically important?

options.A: To prevent the patient from feeling any needle pain
options.B: To stimulate local muscle growth in the limbs
options.C: To prevent lipodystrophy and ensure consistent drug absorption
options.D: To speed up the renal clearance of the medication

explanation: Rotating sites prevents abnormal fat buildup under the skin, which can erraticize how insulin is absorbed. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h6)

question: The primary goal of community-based diabetes screening programs is to...

options.A: provide free lifetime medication to all citizens
options.B: diagnose rare genetic disorders in newborns
options.C: detect hyperglycemia early before complications develop
options.D: eliminate the need for hospital-based doctors

explanation: Screening campaigns catch elevated blood sugar early, allowing for timely intervention and reduced complication risks. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h7)

question: Which strategy is most effective for primary prevention of Type 2 diabetes in communities?

options.A: Promoting healthy diet and regular physical exercise
options.B: Distributing emergency insulin kits to every household
options.C: Isolating diagnosed patients from the general public
options.D: Mandating daily blood tests for all school children

explanation: Lifestyle modifications focusing on diet and exercise successfully prevent or delay the onset of Type 2 diabetes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h7)

question: Diabetic retinopathy is a chronic microvascular complication that specifically damages the...

options.A: peripheral nerves of the lower limbs
options.B: large coronary arteries of the heart
options.C: blood vessels in the retina of the eye
options.D: filtration glomeruli within the kidneys

explanation: Retinopathy involves damage to the small blood vessels supplying the retina, threatening vision. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h8)

question: Why does peripheral neuropathy increase the risk of foot ulcers in diabetic patients?

options.A: Nerve damage directly causes the skin to dissolve overnight
options.B: It completely stops blood flow to the lower extremities
options.C: Loss of protective sensation prevents patients from noticing minor injuries
options.D: It forces patients to walk with an abnormal posture

explanation: When sensation is lost, patients may step on sharp objects or develop blisters without feeling pain, leading to unnoticed wounds. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T3#GNS313_U3_T3_h8)

question: What term describes using a medication for a purpose other than its intended use?

options.A: Addiction recovery
options.B: Physical dependence
options.C: Tolerance building
options.D: Substance misuse

explanation: Substance misuse specifically refers to taking drugs or medicines for reasons or in ways other than what they were prescribed or intended for. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h1)

question: A patient shows physiological adaptation and experiences withdrawal symptoms upon stopping a drug. What does this indicate?

options.A: Casual use
options.B: Dependence
options.C: Misuse
options.D: Tolerance

explanation: Dependence is characterized by physical and psychological changes that cause withdrawal signs when the substance intake stops. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h1)

question: Which category of psychoactive substances slows down central nervous system activity?

options.A: Stimulants
options.B: Hallucinogens
options.C: Depressants
options.D: Cannabinoids

explanation: Depressants reduce brain activity, leading to lowered heart rate, sedation, and slowed reflexes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h2)

question: A young man presenting in the emergency ward has an extremely rapid heart rate, high blood pressure, and agitation after taking an illicit substance. Which drug class is most likely responsible?

options.A: Stimulants
options.B: Depressants
options.C: Sedatives
options.D: Opioids

explanation: Stimulants speed up the nervous system, causing signs like elevated heart rate, high blood pressure, and intense alertness or agitation. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h2)

question: What is a major environmental risk factor for substance abuse among young people in the community?

options.A: Peer pressure
options.B: High income
options.C: Balanced diet
options.D: Regular exercise

explanation: Peer pressure strongly influences adolescents and young adults to try and continue using psychoactive substances to fit into social circles. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h3)

question: Why do individuals with untreated mental health conditions sometimes turn to illicit substances?

options.A: To improve their physical endurance
options.B: To cure their underlying brain infection
options.C: To balance their daily vitamin intake
options.D: To self-medicate their symptoms

explanation: People often use drugs to find temporary relief from painful emotional or psychological distress when professional mental health care is unavailable. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h3)

question: Which neurotransmitter is primarily involved in the brain's reward pathway affected by addictive substances?

options.A: Histamine
options.B: Acetylcholine
options.C: Dopamine
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Dopamine is the key chemical messenger responsible for feelings of pleasure and reinforcement in the brain's reward system. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h4)

question: What causes a person with substance dependence to require larger doses over time to achieve the same effect?

options.A: Overdose
options.B: Withdrawal
options.C: Tolerance
options.D: Metabolism

explanation: Tolerance develops when repeated drug use desensitizes brain receptors, forcing the person to take more of the substance to get the original effect. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which behavioral sign is commonly observed in a client experiencing active substance abuse?

options.A: Increased interest in family bonding
options.B: Consistent early morning punctuality
options.C: Strict adherence to financial budgets
options.D: Sudden mood swings and secretiveness

explanation: Substance abuse often causes noticeable changes in behavior, including unpredictable moods, irritability, and hiding actions from loved ones. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why is patient denial a common challenge when assessing someone for substance abuse?

options.A: Their brain has forgotten how to speak
options.B: Physical tests make denial impossible
options.C: They always remember their exact daily intake
options.D: They may fear social stigma or legal consequences

explanation: Stigma, shame, and fear of punishment often cause individuals to hide their habits or deny having a problem during health assessments. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of using the CAGE questionnaire in community nursing?

options.A: To test physical strength
options.B: To diagnose infectious diseases
options.C: To screen for potential alcohol abuse
options.D: To measure blood sugar levels

explanation: The CAGE questionnaire is a brief, effective tool used by nurses to screen individuals for signs of problem drinking. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h6)

question: A community nurse identifies that a client uses drugs every time they face financial stress. Which nursing diagnosis best fits this situation?

options.A: Ineffective Coping
options.B: Deficient Fluid Volume
options.C: Risk for Infection
options.D: Ineffective Thermoregulation

explanation: Using substances as a primary method to handle daily stressors indicates that the client lacks healthy, adaptive coping mechanisms. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of the detoxification phase in substance abuse treatment?

options.A: To safely manage acute withdrawal symptoms
options.B: To provide permanent housing support
options.C: To cure underlying chronic illnesses
options.D: To teach vocational skills for employment

explanation: Detoxification clears the drug from the body while keeping the patient safe and stable through the dangerous withdrawal phase. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h7)

question: Why is medical supervision necessary when withdrawing from heavy alcohol dependence?

options.A: Patients always sleep through the entire process
options.B: Medical staff must restrict all fluid intake
options.C: Sudden cessation can cause severe, life-threatening seizures
options.D: Withdrawal symptoms never occur without drugs

explanation: Alcohol withdrawal can trigger dangerous physiological reactions, including delirium tremens and seizures, requiring careful medical monitoring. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h7)

question: Which Nigerian agency is primarily responsible for enforcing drug control policies and arresting traffickers?

options.A: NYSC
options.B: NDLEA
options.C: NAFDAC
options.D: FMOH

explanation: The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) is tasked with combating drug trafficking and enforcing laws against illicit substances in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h8)

question: What is a key preventive role for community health nurses addressing substance abuse?

options.A: Educating youth on the risks of drug use
options.B: Importing controlled medications from abroad
options.C: Managing police stations in the local area
options.D: Issuing licenses to pharmaceutical shops

explanation: Community health nurses protect vulnerable populations by spreading awareness, teaching healthy coping skills, and correcting common drug myths. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T4#GNS313_U3_T4_h8)

question: How quickly does nicotine reach the brain after inhaling cigarette smoke?

options.A: After one full day
options.B: After several hours
options.C: Within seconds
options.D: Within thirty minutes

explanation: Inhaled nicotine enters the pulmonary circulation and crosses the blood-brain barrier almost immediately, causing a rapid physiological response. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h1)

question: What is the primary role of dopamine release in nicotine addiction?

options.A: It lowers blood pressure to calm the central nervous system
options.B: It reinforces the habit by creating a pleasurable sensation
options.C: It prevents physical withdrawal symptoms from ever occurring
options.D: It permanently repairs damaged lung tissue in smokers

explanation: The sudden surge of dopamine in the brain acts as a chemical reward, which trains the brain to repeat the smoking behavior. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h1)

question: Which alternative tobacco product has seen a rise in use among urban Nigerian youth?

options.A: Crude snuff powders
options.B: Nicotine-free herbal cigars
options.C: Chewing tobacco leaves
options.D: Shisha waterpipes

explanation: Urban youth increasingly consume tobacco through waterpipes, often mistakenly believing it is safer than conventional cigarettes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h2)

question: A community health nurse in Lagos designs a campaign focusing on rising youth tobacco trends. Which health issue should be prioritized based on current Nigerian epidemiology?

options.A: Non-communicable diseases like lung cancer and heart conditions
options.B: Bacterial respiratory infections transmitted directly through shisha hoses
options.C: Nutritional deficiencies resulting from decreased appetite in smokers
options.D: Acute dehydration caused by heavy waterpipe vapor inhalation

explanation: Long-term tobacco exposure via any method significantly elevates the incidence of chronic non-communicable diseases in the population. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h2)

question: What is the primary effect of cigarette smoke on the respiratory cilia?

options.A: It stimulates them to grow longer and move faster
options.B: It converts them permanently into alveolar air sacs
options.C: It neutralizes all inhaled bacteria without mucus help
options.D: It paralyzes them, preventing effective mucus clearance

explanation: Toxins in cigarette smoke damage and paralyze respiratory cilia, which traps secretions and debris inside the airways. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h3)

question: How does tobacco smoking directly contribute to cardiovascular disease?

options.A: By dilating peripheral blood vessels and dropping blood pressure
options.B: By promoting atherosclerosis and increasing blood platelet stickiness
options.C: By increasing high-density lipoprotein cholesterol levels in blood
options.D: By stopping the heart from beating irregularly during rest periods

explanation: Chemicals in smoke damage arterial linings and encourage clot formation, severely restricting blood flow to vital organs. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h3)

question: What term describes environmental cues like morning tea or stress that prompt a smoker to light up?

options.A: Triggers
options.B: Pathogens
options.C: Allergens
options.D: Placebos

explanation: Triggers are conditioned cues in the environment or emotional state that reliably spark the urge to use tobacco. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why is psychological dependence often harder to break than physical withdrawal alone?

options.A: Because smoking is tied to daily routines and emotional coping
options.B: Because nicotine stays stored inside fat cells for several years
options.C: Because psychological cravings cannot be reduced by counseling
options.D: Because the brain stops producing all natural neurotransmitters

explanation: Behavioral habits are reinforced hundreds of times a day across various life situations, making them deeply ingrained routines. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h4)

question: What is the first step a nurse should take during a routine patient tobacco assessment?

options.A: Order a comprehensive chest X-ray examination
options.B: Refer the client to a psychiatric specialist
options.C: Immediately prescribe nicotine replacement patches
options.D: Ask and document current tobacco use status

explanation: Systematic identification begins by simply asking every patient about their tobacco use habits during intake. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h5)

question: Why is calculating pack-years important when evaluating a long-term smoker?

options.A: It proves whether the patient is ready to stop smoking today
options.B: It measures the exact amount of money spent on cigarettes
options.C: It quantifies cumulative lifetime exposure and disease risk
options.D: It determines the precise daily caloric intake of the client

explanation: Pack-years give healthcare providers a clear metric of total tobacco exposure, helping estimate the likelihood of chronic disease. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h5)

question: Which component of the 5 As framework involves helping the patient set a specific quit date?

options.A: Advise
options.B: Assist
options.C: Assess
options.D: Arrange

explanation: The 'Assist' step involves practical problem-solving, setting a quit date, and developing coping strategies for withdrawal. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h6)

question: When should a nurse use the 5 Rs motivational counseling approach instead of the 5 As?

options.A: When the patient is not yet ready to quit smoking
options.B: When the patient experiences severe acute nicotine withdrawal
options.C: When the patient requests pharmaceutical nicotine replacements
options.D: When the patient has already successfully stopped smoking

explanation: The 5 Rs are designed to enhance motivation for patients who are ambivalent or currently unwilling to make a quit attempt. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of using Nicotine Replacement Therapy during cessation?

options.A: To ease withdrawal symptoms without toxic cigarette tars
options.B: To permanently replace natural dopamine production in the brain
options.C: To cure chronic bronchitis and clear paralyzed lung cilia
options.D: To completely eliminate the psychological habit of smoking

explanation: NRT provides a controlled dose of clean nicotine to relieve physical cravings while avoiding the harmful combustion products of smoking. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h7)

question: How do non-nicotine prescription medications like varenicline assist patients trying to quit?

options.A: By inducing a mild allergic reaction whenever tobacco smoke is smelled
options.B: By binding to brain receptors to reduce cravings and block pleasure
options.C: By increasing blood pressure to prevent drowsiness during the day
options.D: By physically coating the stomach lining to block nicotine absorption

explanation: These medications occupy nicotine receptors in the brain, which lessens withdrawal discomfort and diminishes the reward if a cigarette is smoked. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h7)

question: Which public health policy measure is known to be particularly effective at discouraging youth from starting smoking?

options.A: Allowing indoor smoking areas in public buildings
options.B: Providing free matches with every cigarette pack
options.C: Removing warning labels to reduce consumer anxiety
options.D: Increasing tobacco product taxation and prices

explanation: Higher prices, especially taxes, make tobacco products less affordable for price-sensitive populations like adolescents and young adults. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h8)

question: A public health nurse wants to protect citizens from secondhand smoke in local markets. Which policy should the nurse advocate for?

options.A: Distribution of free pocket ashtrays to all active smokers
options.B: Enforcement of smoke-free zones in public gathering spaces
options.C: Establishment of smoking lounges inside primary health clinics
options.D: Reduction of import tariffs on low-tar cigarette brands

explanation: Smoke-free public policies protect non-smokers from the proven dangers of secondhand smoke exposure in communal areas. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T5#GNS313_U3_T5_h8)

question: What term describes the cumulative physical wear and tear caused by long-term stress?

options.A: Acute distress
options.B: Allostatic load
options.C: Homeostatic drift
options.D: Eustress phase

explanation: Allostatic load measures how chronic exposure to stress hormones damages body systems over time. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why is eustress considered beneficial to human health?

options.A: It completely prevents the release of cortisol in the body
options.B: It motivates individuals and helps them adapt to challenges
options.C: It eliminates all daily environmental demands permanently
options.D: It triggers immediate physical exhaustion and deep sleep

explanation: Eustress provides positive mental stimulation that drives productivity and goal achievement without causing harm. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h1)

question: Which hormone is primarily released by the adrenal cortex during a prolonged stress response?

options.A: Thyroxine
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Cortisol
options.D: Estrogen

explanation: Cortisol is a key glucocorticoid released during the prolonged stress response to maintain energy balance. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h2)

question: A patient under severe chronic stress presents with frequent infections. What explains this finding?

options.A: Direct destruction of antibodies by elevated sympathetic nerve activity
options.B: Rapid dehydration leading to a loss of circulating lymphocytes
options.C: Enhanced white blood cell production from increased adrenaline
options.D: Suppression of the immune system caused by long-term cortisol exposure

explanation: Prolonged high levels of cortisol suppress immune function, making the individual more vulnerable to infections. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h2)

question: What is the correct sequence of stages in Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome?

options.A: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion
options.B: Resistance, alarm, exhaustion
options.C: Alarm, exhaustion, resistance
options.D: Exhaustion, alarm, resistance

explanation: The GAS model starts with the alarm reaction, moves to adaptation or resistance, and ends in exhaustion if the stress continues. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h3)

question: What happens to a patient's body during the resistance stage of stress?

options.A: Energy reserves become completely depleted within a few minutes
options.B: The body attempts to adapt and cope with the ongoing stressor
options.C: The sympathetic nervous system shuts down all vital functions
options.D: Immune defenses operate at maximum efficiency without any cost

explanation: In the resistance stage, the body tries to find a new balance while continuing to fight the stressor. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h3)

question: What is a major localized trigger of chronic stress for many individuals in Nigerian communities?

options.A: Excessive availability of public recreational parks
options.B: Socioeconomic hardship and financial instability
options.C: Oversupply of electricity in urban residential areas
options.D: Strict adherence to strict midday siesta schedules

explanation: Financial struggles, unemployment, and economic instability are major everyday stressors in local communities. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h4)

question: Why must community health nurses understand local environmental stressors in Nigeria?

options.A: To provide culturally relevant and practical care plans for patients
options.B: To enforce strict government policies on urban housing development
options.C: To diagnose rare genetic disorders affecting the nervous system
options.D: To replace traditional healers in treating severe psychiatric illnesses

explanation: Understanding specific local challenges helps nurses design realistic and effective interventions for their patients. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h4)

question: Which validated tool is commonly used by healthcare workers to screen for stress levels?

options.A: Braden risk scale
options.B: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.C: Apgar scoring system
options.D: Perceived Stress Scale

explanation: The Perceived Stress Scale is a widely accepted instrument used to measure how unpredictable and overloaded individuals find their lives. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h5)

question: A patient comes to the clinic complaining of recurring insomnia, tension headaches, and body pains with no clear physical cause. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: End-stage renal failure requiring immediate dialysis
options.B: Severe electrolyte imbalance from excessive hydration
options.C: Unmanaged psychological stress manifesting physically
options.D: Acute bacterial infection of the upper airway

explanation: Physical symptoms like headaches, body pains, and sleep issues are frequent somatic manifestations of high stress. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h5)

question: What type of coping mechanism directly targets and attempts to alter the root cause of a stressor?

options.A: Emotion-focused coping
options.B: Problem-focused coping
options.C: Defensive denial strategy
options.D: Avoidant coping behavior

explanation: Problem-focused coping involves taking direct action to solve or eliminate the source of stress. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h6)

question: How does personal resilience help an individual dealing with community-level hardships?

options.A: It allows the person to adapt and recover from adversity more effectively
options.B: It automatically lowers blood pressure and heart rate permanently
options.C: It completely prevents any future exposure to stressful life events
options.D: It eliminates the need for any social support or community networks

explanation: Resilience is the capacity to withstand and bounce back successfully from difficult life circumstances. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is an effective community-level nursing intervention for reducing social isolation and stress?

options.A: Enforcing mandatory bed rest for all adults
options.B: Establishing local peer support groups
options.C: Isolating stressed individuals from family members
options.D: Prescribing high-dose sedatives to the entire community

explanation: Support groups provide shared understanding, reduce isolation, and foster collective coping strategies in the community. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why is nurse-led stress education valuable in primary healthcare settings?

options.A: It equips individuals with practical self-care and coping skills
options.B: It guarantees complete immunity against chronic physical diseases
options.C: It ensures patients never experience stressful life events again
options.D: It replaces the need for any diagnostic laboratory testing

explanation: Education empowers patients to recognize triggers early and apply healthy management techniques before burnout occurs. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T6#GNS313_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why are micronutrient deficiencies commonly referred to as hidden hunger?

options.A: Affected individuals look healthy while lacking essential vitamins and minerals.
options.B: The body hides these nutrients in fat tissues during times of famine.
options.C: Laboratory tests cannot detect missing minerals in the bloodstream.
options.D: Symptoms only appear during old age after years of accumulation.

explanation: Hidden hunger occurs when calorie intake is sufficient, but vital micronutrients are missing, making malnutrition hard to spot visually. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h1)

question: Which demographic group bears the highest burden of micronutrient deficiencies in Nigeria?

options.A: Elderly farmers in rural communities
options.B: Adolescent males in boarding schools
options.C: Pregnant women and young children
options.D: Working-class adults in urban centers

explanation: Rapid growth phases and high physiological demands make mothers and young children the most vulnerable to micronutrient shortages. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h1)

question: A dietary shortage of iodine primarily leads to the enlargement of which gland?

options.A: Thyroid gland
options.B: Pituitary gland
options.C: Salivary gland
options.D: Adrenal gland

explanation: Iodine is a necessary building block for thyroid hormones, and a shortage forces the gland to swell, forming a goiter. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h2)

question: What is the primary clinical consequence of chronic iron deficiency in young children?

options.A: Impaired cognitive development and fatigue
options.B: Delayed sexual maturation and stunting
options.C: Night blindness and dry corneas
options.D: Enlargement of the thyroid gland

explanation: Iron is needed for oxygen transport in the blood, so its absence reduces energy levels and slows brain development. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h2)

question: How do intestinal parasites contribute directly to micronutrient deficiencies in children?

options.A: By altering the child's genetic makeup permanently
options.B: By forcing the liver to store excess toxic minerals
options.C: By increasing nutrient loss and blocking intestinal absorption
options.D: By destroying the body's ability to produce red blood cells

explanation: Helminths and gut infections sap nutrients directly from the host and damage the intestinal lining, preventing proper absorption. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h3)

question: What is a major dietary contributor to hidden hunger in rural farming households?

options.A: Excessive consumption of imported canned goods
options.B: Eating too many protein-rich animal products
options.C: Heavy reliance on a single starchy staple crop
options.D: Frequent intake of vitamin-fortified beverages

explanation: Diets dominated by one carbohydrate source lack the diverse vitamins and minerals found in varied foods. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h3)

question: Which clinical sign is most characteristic of severe Vitamin A deficiency in children?

options.A: Swelling of the thyroid gland
options.B: Bleeding gums and loose teeth
options.C: Dry corneas and night blindness
options.D: Weakness in the lower limbs

explanation: Vitamin A maintains the health of epithelial tissues and retinal pigments, so its absence leads directly to ocular damage. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h4)

question: A pregnant woman presents with severe fatigue, pallor, and shortness of breath. Which complication is she most at risk for during delivery?

options.A: Development of a goiter
options.B: Severe bone softening
options.C: Hemorrhage and sepsis
options.D: Permanent night blindness

explanation: Severe anemia reduces oxygen reserves, making the mother unable to tolerate normal blood loss during childbirth, increasing bleeding and infection risks. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h4)

question: What simple tool do community health nurses use to quickly screen children for acute malnutrition during outreach?

options.A: A standard wooden tongue depressor
options.B: Urine dipstick reagent strips
options.C: Sphygmomanometer and stethoscope
options.D: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference tape

explanation: MUAC tapes provide a fast, reliable measurement to identify wasting and malnutrition in community settings without weighing scales. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h5)

question: Why are clinical inspections alone sometimes insufficient for diagnosing early micronutrient deficiencies?

options.A: Community members refuse to let nurses examine their skin and eyes.
options.B: Clinical signs change completely depending on the time of day.
options.C: Internal biochemical changes occur long before outward physical signs appear.
options.D: Physical symptoms look identical for every type of vitamin deficiency.

explanation: Nutrient stores drop and cellular function declines before visible stunting, rashes, or eye changes become apparent. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h5)

question: What public health strategy involves adding essential vitamins and minerals to widely consumed commercial food items?

options.A: Therapeutic supplementation
options.B: Targeted deworming
options.C: Dietary diversification
options.D: Food fortification

explanation: Fortification mixes micronutrients into staple foods like salt or oil during manufacturing to reach whole populations automatically. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h6)

question: Why are routine deworming programs paired with micronutrient interventions for young children?

options.A: To stimulate the child's appetite for starchy foods
options.B: To cure children of inherited genetic blood disorders
options.C: To make the child's skin absorb vitamins faster
options.D: To prevent parasites from consuming the nutrients meant for the child

explanation: Intestinal worms rob the host of ingested food, making deworming necessary for nutritional supplements to work effectively. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h6)

question: A community health nurse notices many mothers feeding infants only thin cassava pap after six months. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Prescribe expensive imported baby formula to every household
options.B: Tell the mothers to stop breastfeeding immediately
options.C: Report the mothers to local authorities for child neglect
options.D: Organize a cooking demonstration using local protein and vitamin sources

explanation: Practical education empowers caregivers to enrich local staples with accessible, nutrient-dense foods without shaming them. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h7)

question: What is a primary nursing responsibility during antenatal care clinics to prevent micronutrient deficiencies?

options.A: Conducting laboratory blood chemistry assays
options.B: Performing surgical correction for goiters
options.C: Distributing iron and folic acid tablets
options.D: Managing industrial food fortification plants

explanation: Nurses routinely provide iron and folic acid supplements during antenatal visits to prevent maternal anemia and birth defects. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h7)

question: What is the genetic inheritance pattern of sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Autosomal recessive inheritance
