options.B: X-linked dominant inheritance
options.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance
options.D: X-linked recessive inheritance

explanation: Sickle cell anaemia requires two abnormal genes, one inherited from each parent, making it an autosomal recessive condition. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h1)

question: What happens to red blood cells in a person with sickle cell anaemia under low oxygen levels?

options.A: They swell and burst open immediately
options.B: They multiply faster in the bloodstream
options.C: They shrink into tiny circular discs
options.D: They become rigid and sickle-shaped

explanation: Low oxygen causes abnormal hemoglobin S to polymerize, turning the flexible red blood cells into stiff, crescent shapes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h1)

question: Which amino acid replaces glutamic acid in the beta-globin chain of sickle hemoglobin?

options.A: Lysine
options.B: Valine
options.C: Alanine
options.D: Glycine

explanation: A single point mutation replaces glutamic acid with valine, altering the physical properties of the hemoglobin molecule. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h2)

question: Why do sickle cells cause damage to body tissues?

options.A: They stick together and block tiny blood vessels
options.B: They dissolve the walls of major arteries
options.C: They produce too much oxygen for the tissues
options.D: They absorb all available white blood cells

explanation: The rigid cells clog microcirculation, cutting off oxygen supply and causing localized tissue damage and pain. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h2)

question: What is the earliest clinical manifestation of sickle cell anaemia usually seen in toddlers?

options.A: Sudden paralysis of the lower limbs
options.B: Complete failure of kidney function
options.C: Painful swelling of the hands and feet
options.D: Yellow discoloration of the eye sclera

explanation: Dactylitis, or hand-foot syndrome, results from vaso-occlusion in the small bones of infants and toddlers. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h3)

question: Why do newborn babies with sickle cell anaemia rarely show symptoms at birth?

options.A: Maternal antibodies completely prevent any sickling crisis
options.B: High levels of fetal hemoglobin protect them initially
options.C: Their bone marrow does not produce red blood cells yet
options.D: The abnormal genes remain dormant until puberty starts

explanation: Fetal hemoglobin does not interact with sickle hemoglobin polymers, delaying symptoms until fetal hemoglobin is replaced by adult hemoglobin. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h3)

question: Which laboratory test provides definitive confirmation of hemoglobin types and variants?

options.A: Packed cell volume screening
options.B: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
options.C: Full blood count analysis
options.D: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate

explanation: Electrophoresis separates different hemoglobin types on a medium using electrical current, confirming the exact genotype. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h4)

question: When is neonatal screening most effectively integrated into routine child healthcare in Nigeria?

options.A: When the child reaches secondary school age
options.B: During routine childhood immunization clinic visits
options.C: During emergency treatment for severe malaria
options.D: Only when the child is admitted for surgery

explanation: Immunization clinics bring in large numbers of infants, offering the best opportunity for early detection and counseling. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the most frequent type of crisis experienced by patients with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Hemolytic crisis
options.B: Splenic sequestration
options.C: Vaso-occlusive crisis
options.D: Aplastic crisis

explanation: Vaso-occlusive crises happen when sickled cells block blood flow, causing severe pain and remaining the most common reason for hospital admission. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h5)

question: Which infection is commonly associated with triggering an aplastic crisis in sickle cell patients?

options.A: Parvovirus B19
options.B: Plasmodium falciparum
options.C: Salmonella typhi
options.D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

explanation: Parvovirus B19 specifically infects red blood cell precursors in the bone marrow, halting red cell production and causing an aplastic crisis. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h5)

question: What is the primary reason for administering intravenous fluids during a vaso-occlusive crisis?

options.A: To reduce blood viscosity and improve microvascular flow
options.B: To prevent the development of high blood pressure
options.C: To completely suppress active bone marrow production
options.D: To raise the body temperature during a fever spike

explanation: Hydration dilutes the blood, lowering viscosity and helping red blood cells pass through narrowed vessels more easily. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h6)

question: A patient in severe sickle cell pain requests medication. What is the best initial nursing action?

options.A: Apply ice packs to the painful joints to reduce local swelling
options.B: Wait until laboratory results confirm the exact hemoglobin level
options.C: Assess pain characteristics and administer prescribed analgesics promptly
options.D: Encourage deep breathing exercises before giving any pain relief

explanation: Prompt pain assessment and medication administration are essential for effective crisis management and patient trust. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h6)

question: How should a nurse conduct genetic counseling for couples planning to marry?

options.A: Advise them to rely entirely on prayer and spiritual fasting
options.B: Tell them to hide their test results from their extended family
options.C: Provide objective genotype information to guide their personal choices
options.D: Instruct them strictly on who they are permitted to marry

explanation: Genetic counseling is non-directive, meaning nurses provide facts and support without making decisions for the clients. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h7)

question: Which preventive measure is routinely recommended for young children diagnosed with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Complete restriction from outdoor sunlight
options.B: Surgical removal of the spleen at birth
options.C: Daily prophylactic antibiotics and antimalarials
options.D: Monthly blood transfusions at the clinic

explanation: Children with sickle cell anaemia take daily prophylactic medications, such as penicillin and antimalarials, to prevent severe infections. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h7)

question: What is the main goal of public health policies addressing sickle cell anaemia in Nigeria?

options.A: To improve early detection, prevention, and quality of life
options.B: To make genetic testing mandatory for all school children
options.C: To isolate affected individuals from the general population
options.D: To replace all traditional medicine with foreign treatments

explanation: Public health policies aim to reduce disease burden through screening, education, accessible treatment, and supportive care. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h8)

question: Which medication is commonly promoted in modern public health guidelines to reduce sickle cell crises?

options.A: Insulin
options.B: Hydroxyurea
options.C: Paracetamol
options.D: Furosemide

explanation: Hydroxyurea stimulates the production of fetal hemoglobin, reducing red blood cell sickling and the frequency of painful crises. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T8#GNS313_U3_T8_h8)

question: What is the most common cancer diagnosed among women in Nigeria?

options.A: Breast cancer
options.B: Liver cancer
options.C: Cervical cancer
options.D: Ovarian cancer

explanation: Breast cancer has the highest incidence rates among women both locally in Nigeria and across global populations. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h1)

question: Why do many Nigerian women present with advanced stages of breast cancer at healthcare facilities?

options.A: Local hospitals completely lack any diagnostic tools
options.B: Financial constraints and cultural beliefs delaying care
options.C: The disease grows much faster in African populations
options.D: Early symptoms only appear during the terminal stage

explanation: Delays in seeking orthodox treatment are frequently linked to economic barriers, fear, and reliance on traditional remedies. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h1)

question: Which anatomical structure provides main structural support and shape to the breast?

options.A: Lactiferous ducts
options.B: Areolar glands
options.C: Cooper's ligaments
options.D: Pectoralis major muscle

explanation: Cooper's suspensory ligaments connect the breast tissue to the dermis, providing structural support. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h2)

question: Where do the majority of breast malignancies typically originate?

options.A: The external nipple skin
options.B: Terminal duct lobular units
options.C: Fatty adipose tissue layers
options.D: Cooper's suspensory ligaments

explanation: Most breast cancers start in the epithelial cells lining the ducts and lobules of the glandular tissue. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h2)

question: Which genetic mutations are strongly linked to an increased risk of hereditary breast cancer?

options.A: CDK4 and RB1
options.B: BRCA1 and BRCA2
options.C: HER2 and PIK3CA
options.D: TP53 and EGFR

explanation: Inherited mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes significantly elevate lifetime breast cancer risk. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h3)

question: Prolonged exposure to which hormone is a primary driver in many breast cancer cases?

options.A: Cortisol
options.B: Thyroxine
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Estrogen

explanation: Extended lifetime exposure to estrogen, from early periods or late menopause, stimulates cellular proliferation in breast tissue. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h3)

question: What is the key difference between in situ and invasive breast cancer?

options.A: Invasive cancer only affects the skin of the nipple
options.B: In situ cancer immediately spreads to distant organs
options.C: In situ cells have not breached the basement membrane
options.D: Invasive cancer is entirely benign and non-cancerous

explanation: Carcinoma in situ is confined within the duct or lobule, whereas invasive carcinoma breaks through into surrounding tissue. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h4)

question: What does the letter 'N' stand for in the TNM cancer staging system?

options.A: Number of mitotic cells
options.B: Necrosis of the tumor
options.C: Nuclear grade severity
options.D: Lymph node involvement

explanation: In the TNM classification, N describes the extent of spread to regional lymph nodes. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h4)

question: Which physical characteristic describes a typical malignant breast lump found during palpation?

options.A: Warm, tender, and fluctuating
options.B: Hard, painless, and irregular in shape
options.C: Soft, mobile, and painful on touch
options.D: Cystic, fluid-filled, and smooth

explanation: Malignant lumps are typically firm to hard, painless, fixed, and possess irregular borders. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h5)

question: What is the medical term for the dimpled, thickened skin appearance caused by lymphatic blockage in breast cancer?

options.A: Erythema multiforme
options.B: Psoriasis vulgaris
options.C: Lichen planus
options.D: Peau d'orange

explanation: Edema from blocked dermal lymphatics creates an orange-peel skin texture known as peau d'orange. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h5)

question: When is the best time for a menstruating woman to perform a breast self-examination?

options.A: On the first day of menstrual bleeding
options.B: Right before her menstrual bleeding starts
options.C: During the middle of her ovulation cycle
options.D: A few days after her monthly period ends

explanation: Hormonal swelling subsides after menstruation, making the breast tissue soft and easier to examine accurately. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h6)

question: Why is breast ultrasonography often preferred over mammography for younger women?

options.A: Mammography machines are completely unavailable in all health centers
options.B: Ultrasound can fully replace the need for tissue biopsies
options.C: Ultrasound uses high-dose radiation to kill cancer cells
options.D: Younger women have dense breast tissue that hides details on X-rays

explanation: Dense breast tissue limits mammogram sensitivity, making ultrasound an effective complementary imaging tool. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h6)

question: What is a key nursing intervention to prevent lymphedema after a left modified radical mastectomy?

options.A: Encourage heavy weightlifting exercises with the left arm
options.B: Elevate the left arm above the heart level all day
options.C: Apply tight elastic bandages continuously to the left hand
options.D: Avoid blood pressure measurements on the left arm

explanation: Avoiding trauma, venipuncture, and blood pressure measurements on the affected side prevents impaired lymphatic flow and lymphedema. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h7)

question: Which surgical procedure involves the removal of the entire breast tissue along with axillary lymph nodes?

options.A: Partial lumpectomy
options.B: Excisional biopsy
options.C: Simple cosmetic reduction
options.D: Modified radical mastectomy

explanation: A modified radical mastectomy removes the entire breast along with regional lymph nodes in the axilla. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of palliative care for a patient with terminal breast cancer?

options.A: Speeding up the natural terminal dying process
options.B: Curing the primary malignancy through aggressive chemotherapy
options.C: Improving quality of life and controlling distressing symptoms
options.D: Reversing distant organ metastasis in the liver and lungs

explanation: Palliative care focuses on relieving pain and suffering to ensure the best possible quality of life. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h8)

question: Which guideline framework is typically used to manage cancer pain effectively?

options.A: APGAR scoring system
options.B: TNM staging scale
options.C: Glasgow coma scale
options.D: WHO analgesic ladder

explanation: The World Health Organization analgesic ladder guides the stepwise administration of pain relief medications. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h8)

question: How do nurses contribute most effectively to secondary prevention of breast cancer in Nigeria?

options.A: Isolating diagnosed patients from their local communities
options.B: Performing complex surgical mastectomies in local health centers
options.C: Prescribing chemotherapy drugs during community outreaches
options.D: Conducting awareness campaigns and teaching early detection methods

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection through community screening and education to catch disease early. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h9)

question: Which of the following is an example of a primary prevention strategy for breast cancer?

options.A: Encouraging regular physical exercise and healthy nutrition
options.B: Starting targeted hormonal therapy after surgery
options.C: Scheduling routine screening mammography tests
options.D: Performing a monthly clinical breast examination

explanation: Primary prevention aims to prevent the disease from developing initially through lifestyle modifications. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T9#GNS313_U3_T9_h9)

question: What is the primary focus of epidemiology in community health nursing?

options.A: Studying disease patterns in entire populations
options.B: Managing financial budgets for local health clinics
options.C: Diagnosing rare diseases in hospital laboratories
options.D: Providing bedside nursing care to individual patients

explanation: Epidemiology focuses on tracking diseases and health events across whole groups rather than single individuals. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why is epidemiologic data vital for community health nurses?

options.A: It eliminates the need for physical examinations in clinics
options.B: It replaces the need to interview sick community members
options.C: It guarantees that funding will increase every fiscal year
options.D: It helps plan effective prevention and allocate resources wisely

explanation: Having accurate data allows nurses to target interventions where they are needed most to protect the community. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is an example of secondary epidemiologic data?

options.A: Measuring the mid-upper arm circumference of children
options.B: Interviewing village elders about local health beliefs
options.C: Conducting blood pressure checks at a local market square
options.D: Reviewing past mortality records from the health ministry

explanation: Secondary data refers to information that was already gathered by other agencies or researchers in the past. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h2)

question: A community health nurse conducts a household survey to count active tuberculosis cases. What type of data is this primarily?

options.A: Hypothetical data
options.B: Quantitative data
options.C: Secondary data
options.D: Qualitative data

explanation: Counting active cases involves numerical measurements, which classifies the information as quantitative data. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h2)

question: Which data collection method involves talking directly with trusted village leaders about local health issues?

options.A: Laboratory blood screenings
options.B: Key informant interviews
options.C: Direct environmental observation
options.D: Reviewing census registers

explanation: Key informants are knowledgeable community figures who provide deep insight into local health behaviors and needs. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h3)

question: A nurse wants to assess how community members handle their household drinking water. Which method is most appropriate?

options.A: Calculating annual hospital mortality statistics
options.B: Analyzing international disease journals
options.C: Reading national population census booklets
options.D: Direct observation of water storage practices

explanation: Direct observation allows the nurse to see actual daily behaviors regarding water handling rather than relying on reported answers. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h3)

question: What does the term 'reliability' mean in the context of data collection?

options.A: Getting consistent results if the measurement is repeated
options.B: Collecting information quickly during an emergency
options.C: Storing physical records in a secure steel cabinet
options.D: Ensuring the data matches the exact true value

explanation: Reliability refers to the stability and consistency of data collection tools and methods over multiple uses. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a good way to maintain high data quality?

options.A: Relying entirely on memory without writing down field notes
options.B: Training field staff properly before surveys begin
options.C: Conducting routine spot-checks and data audits
options.D: Using clear and pre-tested data collection forms

explanation: Human memory is fallible; failing to record data immediately in the field leads to severe omissions and errors. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of analyzing epidemiologic data?

options.A: To turn raw numbers into understandable patterns of health
options.B: To replace the need for physical patient examinations
options.C: To make collection forms look neat and professional
options.D: To hide mistakes made during community surveys

explanation: Analysis organizes scattered information so nurses can see where and why health issues are occurring. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h5)

question: A nurse compares the number of malaria cases between two villages with different population sizes. Why is calculating a rate better than just looking at raw counts?

options.A: Rates eliminate the need for laboratory confirmations
options.B: Raw counts are always illegal to use in public health
options.C: Rates account for differences in total population size
options.D: Raw counts are harder to write down on paper forms

explanation: Comparing raw counts alone can be misleading if one village is much larger than the other; rates provide a fair comparison. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h5)

question: When is epidemiologic data considered fully utilised in public health?

options.A: When it drives practical action and health interventions
options.B: When it is printed in a foreign medical textbook
options.C: When field logbooks are completely filled with ink
options.D: When it is locked away safely in a government vault

explanation: Data exists to guide decision-making and solve real community health problems, not just sit on a shelf. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h6)

question: A nurse notices from clinic data that adolescent girls in a rural area have low uptake of tetanus vaccinations. What should be the next step based on data utilization principles?

options.A: Ignore the data because teenagers are generally healthy
options.B: Design a targeted outreach campaign to educate and vaccinate the girls
options.C: Stop collecting vaccination data to save time and energy
options.D: Punish the local clinic staff for failing to report high numbers

explanation: The nurse uses the identified gap in data to direct resources and action toward the unprotected group. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h6)

question: What must a nurse obtain from a community member before conducting an individual health interview or examination?

options.A: Informed consent
options.B: Written tax records
options.C: A financial deposit
options.D: Political clearance

explanation: Every participant has the right to know what a study involves and agree voluntarily before giving personal data. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h7)

question: Why is patient confidentiality especially critical during community health data collection?

options.A: It prevents the government from spending money on printing paper
options.B: It protects personal dignity and maintains community trust in health workers
options.C: It ensures that nurses never have to speak with village leaders
options.D: It makes data analysis much faster for computer software programs

explanation: If people fear their private health details will be exposed, they will hide illnesses and avoid public clinics. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h7)

question: What is a common challenge faced when gathering data in rural community settings?

options.A: Cultural suspicions and logistical barriers like bad roads
options.B: An overabundance of trained epidemiologists in every village
options.C: Having too many computers and electricity sources available
options.D: Patients demanding financial payment for answering questions

explanation: Fieldwork often involves poor infrastructure and occasional mistrust from residents who misunderstand health activities. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h8)

question: How can a community health nurse best address local suspicion regarding health surveys?

options.A: Ignore the suspicious residents and only interview hospital staff
options.B: Collect data secretly at night without telling community members
options.C: Involve respected local leaders and explain the purpose clearly
options.D: Threaten residents with fines if they refuse to answer questions

explanation: Partnering with trusted community figures helps dispel myths and reassures residents that the health activities are safe and beneficial. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T1#GNS313_U4_T1_h8)

question: What are vital statistics primarily records of?

options.A: Life events in a human population
options.B: Financial budgets of local clinics
options.C: Hospital equipment inventory
options.D: Nursing school enrollment numbers

explanation: Vital statistics focus strictly on tracking core life events such as births, deaths, and marriages within a community. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why do community health nurses need to understand vital statistics?

options.A: To diagnose rare diseases in individual patients
options.B: To calculate daily hospital meal portions
options.C: To see the health trends of the entire community
options.D: To manage the financial payroll of the ward

explanation: Looking at population numbers helps nurses understand broader health patterns rather than just focusing on one sick person at a time. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h1)

question: What is the primary legal method for continuously recording births and deaths?

options.A: Household surveys
options.B: Newspaper announcements
options.C: Annual population census
options.D: Civil registration

explanation: Civil registration is the official, continuous government process of recording vital events as they happen in real-time. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h2)

question: When would a community health team rely on a sample survey instead of a census?

options.A: When recording a marriage certificate
options.B: When complete registration is not possible
options.C: When every single citizen comes to the clinic
options.D: When the government wants to count every building

explanation: Sample surveys are used to gather reliable estimates from a smaller group when tracking down every single person is too difficult. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h2)

question: What does a demographic rate typically measure?

options.A: The weight of medical equipment in a ward
options.B: The physical size of a community health center
options.C: The exact total money spent on healthcare
options.D: How often an event happens in a population over time

explanation: Rates show the frequency of specific occurrences, like births or deaths, relative to the total population size over a given period. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h3)

question: A public health nurse wants to measure how many live births occurred per one thousand people in a town over one year. Which rate should be calculated?

options.A: Disease Prevalence Rate
options.B: Crude Birth Rate
options.C: Hospital Admission Ratio
options.D: Maternal Mortality Rate

explanation: The Crude Birth Rate specifically calculates live births per one thousand population in a defined one-year period. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h3)

question: What does morbidity measure in a community?

options.A: The state of being unhealthy or diseased
options.B: The total number of registered deaths
options.C: The number of new babies born in a year
options.D: The amount of money earned by hospitals

explanation: Morbidity focuses on illness, sickness, and disease prevalence rather than death itself. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h4)

question: Why is it important for nurses to study both morbidity and mortality statistics together?

options.A: To prove that nobody gets sick in rural areas
options.B: To replace the need for physical patient examinations
options.C: To see which illnesses cause suffering versus which ones cause death
options.D: To calculate the exact salary of medical doctors

explanation: Looking at both illness rates and death rates provides a complete picture of the total health burden affecting a population. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h4)

question: What does the Infant Mortality Rate measure?

options.A: Babies who die before reaching their first birthday
options.B: Children under five years old who get malaria
options.C: Mothers who die during childbirth
options.D: Total number of babies born in a hospital

explanation: Infant Mortality Rate specifically tracks deaths occurring during the first year of life per one thousand live births. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h5)

question: High rates of under-five mortality in a community usually point to problems with which of the following?

options.A: Preventable infections and nutrition
options.B: Lack of secondary school education for adults
options.C: High rates of retirement among elderly workers
options.D: Excessive spending on surgical equipment

explanation: Child deaths under five are largely driven by malnutrition, poor sanitation, and preventable childhood infectious diseases. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which of the following is a major reason why vital statistics are often incomplete in rural Nigeria?

options.A: Every citizen has a personal digital health computer
options.B: Hospitals refuse to admit pregnant women
options.C: Too many people work as professional statisticians
options.D: Many births and deaths happen at home and go unreported

explanation: Home deliveries and unreported home deaths mean many vital events never make it into official government records. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is a direct consequence of having weak vital data collection systems in a country?

options.A: Doctors will have less paperwork to complete daily
options.B: Citizens will stop falling sick from infectious diseases
options.C: Hospitals will automatically receive excess funding
options.D: Health planners rely on estimates that may lead to poor interventions

explanation: Inaccurate or missing data forces decision-makers to guess where resources are needed, resulting in poorly targeted health programs. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h6)

question: How do health ministries primarily use vital statistics data?

options.A: To test the speed of computer networks in wards
options.B: To decide which medications taste best
options.C: To allocate medical budgets and place facilities
options.D: To grade nursing students on final exams

explanation: Governments use population data to figure out where to spend money and build clinics based on real community needs. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h7)

question: A state health board notices a sharp rise in infant mortality in a rural district through vital data. What action should they take first?

options.A: Increase taxes for citizens living in urban areas
options.B: Close all the primary schools in the affected region
options.C: Stop collecting birth data for the next five years
options.D: Direct more child health resources and immunisation teams to that district

explanation: When data highlights a specific problem area, health planners must channel targeted interventions directly to that community to save lives. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T2#GNS313_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of disease surveillance in public health?

options.A: Providing free medications to impoverished community members
options.B: Conducting clinical trials for newly discovered pharmaceutical drugs
options.C: Continuous monitoring of health events to guide public health action
options.D: Managing hospital budgets and staff shift rosters effectively

explanation: Surveillance is all about watching health trends over time so authorities can take proper action to protect the public. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: How does disease surveillance differ from standard bedside nursing care?

options.A: Surveillance is only performed by doctors inside specialized laboratories
options.B: Surveillance deals exclusively with chronic genetic disorders
options.C: Surveillance requires advanced surgical skills instead of basic bedside observation
options.D: Surveillance focuses on population-level health trends rather than single patients

explanation: While bedside nursing cares for one patient at a time, surveillance looks at the big picture to protect entire communities. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which type of surveillance involves public health workers actively visiting facilities to search for cases?

options.A: Sentinel surveillance
options.B: Active surveillance
options.C: Syndromic surveillance
options.D: Passive surveillance

explanation: Active surveillance means health staff take the initiative to go out and look for cases rather than waiting for reports to come in. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h2)

question: A public health team monitors school absenteeism and pharmacy sales of cough syrup during a flu season. What type of surveillance is this?

options.A: Passive surveillance
options.B: Laboratory surveillance
options.C: Syndromic surveillance
options.D: Sentinel surveillance

explanation: Syndromic surveillance tracks symptom clusters and related data before a formal lab diagnosis is confirmed. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h2)

question: What is the very first step in the disease surveillance process?

options.A: Mass vaccination
options.B: Data collection
options.C: Data dissemination
options.D: Policy creation

explanation: You cannot analyze or interpret what you have not yet collected. Data collection is always the starting point. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h3)

question: Why is the dissemination step crucial in public health surveillance?

options.A: It serves as a legal punishment for hospitals that fail to report cases
options.B: It allows researchers to sell health data to private pharmaceutical companies
options.C: It ensures that useful health information reaches those who need to take action
options.D: It replaces the need for clinical diagnosis in remote rural clinics

explanation: Collecting data is useless if the findings are not shared with the people and leaders who can implement control measures. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following is considered a primary biological data source for disease confirmation?

options.A: Political speeches
options.B: Laboratory records
options.C: Newspaper reports
options.D: Market sales receipts

explanation: Laboratory test results provide the scientific proof needed to confirm the exact organism causing an illness. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why are community sources like traditional healers or school registers important in rural disease surveillance?

options.A: Traditional healers are legally required to manage national epidemics
options.B: Rural schools have better medical laboratories than city hospitals
options.C: Many rural residents may never visit a formal hospital when they first fall ill
options.D: Government health workers are forbidden from working outside cities

explanation: In areas with limited healthcare access, community-level informants catch cases that would otherwise go entirely unrecorded. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of establishing a clear case definition in surveillance?

options.A: Determining the exact cost of hospital treatment for insurance claims
options.B: Speeding up the time it takes to prescribe antibiotics to a patient
options.C: Fulfilling administrative paperwork requirements without clinical value
options.D: Ensuring everyone uses the exact same criteria to identify a disease

explanation: A standard case definition ensures that health workers across different regions are counting the exact same illness criteria. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why must certain dangerous illnesses like yellow fever be reported immediately to national authorities?

options.A: To allow rapid response teams to contain outbreaks before they spread widely
options.B: To ensure the affected patient receives free lifetime medical care
options.C: To permit international travelers to enter the country without restrictions
options.D: To close down all local markets permanently in the affected zone

explanation: Immediate reporting triggers fast public health interventions that can stop a small cluster from turning into a massive epidemic. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h5)

question: Where do community health nurses usually first notice unusual patterns of disease?

options.A: During routine home visits, school check-ups, or clinic duties
options.B: While managing hospital kitchen menus and supply inventories
options.C: During international travel conferences held in capital cities
options.D: While reviewing global financial market reports in an office

explanation: Nurses encounter patients directly in communities and clinics, making them the primary observers of local health changes. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h6)

question: A community nurse notices three children from the same street presenting with high fever and yellow eyes. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Advise the parents to keep the children away from school without notifying anyone
options.B: Report the suspected cases according to local surveillance guidelines and investigate further
options.C: Assume it is a normal seasonal illness and provide standard rest advice at home
options.D: Wait until next month to see if more children in the neighborhood get sick

explanation: Spotting a cluster of serious symptoms requires prompt reporting and investigation to prevent a wider outbreak. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h6)

question: What is the main reason we report certain diseases to public health authorities?

options.A: To bill insurance companies for hospital admissions
options.B: To report specific illnesses to public health authorities
options.C: To track daily hospital staff attendance records
options.D: To update patient medical history in private files

explanation: You got this! Disease notification simply means letting health officials know about dangerous illnesses so they can jump in quickly and stop outbreaks before they spread. Great job! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why is it so important to report a disease outbreak quickly in your community?

options.A: It guarantees free medical treatment for all citizens
options.B: It stops patients from visiting traditional healers
options.C: It helps health agencies spot unusual disease patterns early
options.D: It reduces the cost of prescription drugs in pharmacies

explanation: Spotting cases early gives health teams the heads-up they need to track trends and stop epidemics in their tracks. You're building solid public health sense! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h1)

question: How can we best describe public health surveillance?

options.A: A method for punishing clinics that lose patient files
options.B: A financial audit of private clinic expenditures
options.C: An ongoing system of collecting and analyzing health data
options.D: A one-time yearly census of hospital bed capacity

explanation: Think of surveillance as a continuous watch, not just a one-off check. We keep gathering and reviewing health data day in and day out to stay ahead of sickness! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h2)

question: During a health emergency, how do health ministries use surveillance data?

options.A: To allocate scarce medical resources where they are needed most
options.B: To select which nursing students receive scholarships
options.C: To decide which private hospitals should be closed permanently
options.D: To determine salary increases for hospital administrators

explanation: Good data shows us exactly where an outbreak is hitting hardest. That way, we can rush medications, supplies, and staff right where they'll save the most lives. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h2)

question: Which type of diseases must be reported the absolute fastest because they can spark sudden outbreaks?

options.A: Routine dental health issues
options.B: Epidemic-prone diseases
options.C: Surgical complication records
options.D: Chronic nutritional deficiencies

explanation: Diseases like cholera or measles move fast! We call these epidemic-prone, and they need immediate reporting so we can protect the community. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h3)

question: A nurse identifies a case of polio. Why do we place polio in a special, urgent reporting category?

options.A: It is a targeted disease for global eradication and elimination
options.B: It only affects elderly patients in urban hospitals
options.C: It is a common seasonal allergy with mild symptoms
options.D: It does not require tracking by government agencies

explanation: The world is actively trying to wipe out polio completely. Because every single case is a global emergency, we track them with extreme urgency! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h3)

question: Who starts the whole disease-reporting chain right at the grassroots level?

options.A: The administrative clerk in charge of billing
options.B: The frontline nurse or doctor who assesses the patient
options.C: The international health organization representative
options.D: The federal minister of health in the capital city

explanation: That's you! The nurse or clinician at the bedside or clinic floor who first sees the patient is always the crucial first link in the reporting chain. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h4)

question: If a nurse at a rural primary health center diagnoses Lassa fever, who must be notified immediately next in the reporting chain?

options.A: The federal ministry of finance budget office
options.B: The national television broadcasting station
options.C: The Local Government Area surveillance officer
options.D: The World Health Organization headquarters overseas

explanation: Reporting flows step-by-step from the local clinic straight to the Local Government Area (LGA) team before heading to the state and national levels. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h4)

question: What standard framework guides disease reporting forms in Nigerian health facilities?

options.A: Standard Operating Procedures for Pharmacy Inventory
options.B: National Curriculum for Basic Nursing Education
options.C: Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR)
options.D: International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS)

explanation: IDSR is the golden framework we use across Nigerian facilities to keep our disease tracking organized and consistent. You'll see this a lot in practice! [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is a common mistake nurses should avoid when suspecting a notifiable disease outbreak?

options.A: Informing the local government health team too quickly
options.B: Using standard case definition sheets during patient assessment
options.C: Waiting for full laboratory confirmation before reporting the suspect case
options.D: Submitting weekly summary logs to public health authorities

explanation: Never wait for lab results if you suspect a dangerous outbreak! Report based on clinical signs right away so health teams can act fast. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h5)

question: What is the main goal of 'active case finding' during an outbreak?

options.A: To conduct routine training for nursing students
options.B: To audit the financial accounts of the local hospital
options.C: To replace expired medications in the pharmacy store
options.D: To search for additional unrecorded cases in the community

explanation: Instead of waiting for sick people to walk into the clinic, active case finding means going out into the community to find anyone else who might be hiding or missing treatment. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why do public health teams collect blood or stool samples during a suspected outbreak?

options.A: To test the quality of local drinking water pipes only
options.B: To measure the general nutritional status of healthy adults
options.C: To calculate the daily operational costs of the clinic
options.D: To identify the specific causative agent in a laboratory

explanation: Lab tests on these samples tell us the exact germ, bacteria, or virus causing the trouble, helping us choose the exact right treatment. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why are community health nurses usually the first to notice an unusual disease cluster?

options.A: Because they only review paperwork sent from foreign countries
options.B: Because they spend all their time working in national research labs
options.C: Because they focus entirely on hospital financial accounting
options.D: Because they interact daily with families and local groups

explanation: Community nurses are right on the ground! Because you work closely with local families every day, you're in the best position to spot when something feels off. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h7)

question: How can nurses help stop community members from hiding infectious illnesses out of fear?

options.A: Refusing to treat patients who do not speak English
options.B: Keeping all health information secret from local leaders
options.C: Threatening penalties for families that miss immunization days
options.D: Building trust through health education and supportive care

explanation: When we show empathy, educate gently, and create a safe space without judgment, community members feel comfortable coming to us early. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h7)

question: What is a common hurdle that slows down prompt disease reporting in resource-limited settings?

options.A: Excessive availability of advanced laboratory computers
options.B: Too many trained surveillance officers in every clinic
options.C: Zero workload for nurses during morning shifts
options.D: Shortage of reporting forms and poor transport

explanation: Logistical challenges like running out of paper forms or lacking transport to deliver them can unfortunately drag down reporting times. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T4#GNS313_U4_T4_h8)

question: How can health facilities best fix the problem of staff underreporting due to a fear of blame?

options.A: By firing every nurse who makes a minor documentation error
options.B: By hiding all disease statistics from the government ministry
